Uniform Title: *Bhuvaneśvarīmahāstotra* Author: Pṛthvīdharācārya Commentator: Kavi Padmanābha
Editor: Gopal Narayan Bahura Description: Description by Mark S.G. Dyczkowski:
The *Bhuvaneśvarīmahāstotra* by Pṛthvīdharācārya, together with [its commentary].
Under the title *Kavi Padmanābha’s Commentary*, edited by Gopāl Nārāyaṇ Bahura,
the editor presents a collection of texts related to Bhuvaneśvarī and her worship, drawn from several manuscripts. These...
1) *Bhuvaneśvarīmahāstotra* by Pṛthvīdharācārya, with a commentary by Kavi Padmanābha.
2) *Rudrayāmalīyabhuvaneśvarīpañcāṅga*:
This is a chapter (*paṭala*) from the *Daśavidyārahasya*, which is said to be a part of the *Rudrayāmala*.
3) Bhuvaneśvarīpūjāpaddhatiḥ:
This is the manual for the regular daily worship (*nityapūjanapaddhati*) of Bhuvaneśvarī, extracted from the *Daśavidyārahasya*.
4) *Bhuvaneśvarīkavaca*, titled *Trailokyamaṅgala*, attributed to the *Rudrayāmala*.
3) *Bhuvaneśvarīsahasranāmastotra*, attributed to the *Rudrayāmala*.
4) *Bhuvaneśvaryaṣṭottaraśatanāmastotra*, attributed to the *Rudrayāmala*.
5) *Bhuvaneśvaryaṣṭakam* 6) *Bhuvaneśvarīsahasranāmastotram*, attributed to the *Mahātantrārṇava* 7) *Bhuvaneśvarīhṛdayastotram*, attributed to the *Nīlasarasvatītantra*
8) *Bhuvaneśvarīstotra*, attributed to the *Rudrayāmala*;
9) A text by Pṛthvīdharācārya, together with its commentary titled *Bhuvaneśvarīkramacandrikā* by Anantadeva of Mātṛpura, who belonged to...
to the lineage of Dāyīdeva. There are three chapters (*kalpa*) concerning the daily rites dedicated to the goddess Bhuvaneśvarī.
10) *Laghusaptaśatīstotram*: a brief hymn to Caṇḍikā based on [the *Saptaśatī*].
In his introduction, the editor presents Pṛthvīdharācārya as a direct disciple of Śaṅkarācārya, whom he dates to the [eighth] century CE.

Ninth century. Although Pṛthvīdharācārya may have been a *saṃnyāsin* belonging to that order, it is impossible for him to have lived so early. Bhuvaneśvarī is one of the Ten Mahāvidyās. Indeed, two of...

The texts in this collection consist of a *paṭala* from the *Daśavidyārahasya*, which is said to be a part of the *Rudrayāmala*. Four other works are attributed directly to the *Rudrayāmala*. Regarding the practice of...
Attributing revelation to this work is common in the later period.
The *Nīlasarasvatītantra* is certainly late, as is most likely the *Mahātantrārṇava*. As for the grouping and worship of the ten goddesses...
The group that constitutes the Ten Mahāvidyās is very popular in North India,
where temples and shrines dedicated to them are found in several northern cities as well as in the Kathmandu Valley. However, although these goddesses are...

They are known in the South, yet they are not worshipped there as members of this group. The texts in which they appear together do not date back earlier than the fifteenth century, and their introduction into Nepal is likely even later.

The Great Hymn to Bhuvaneśvarī, composed by the illustrious Pṛthvīdhara Ācārya, the sovereign of all the teachers of the Āgamas.
Adorned with the commentary composed by Kavipadmanābha.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Oṃ! The Mother, resplendent with ornaments of shimmering pearls and gold, is clothed in exceedingly red garments.
May that Goddess Bhuvaneśvarī— who has slender limbs, who is exceedingly beautiful with three eyes, who shines like the rising sun,
whose hands are adorned with a divine goad and noose, who always removes fear, and who dwells within our hearts— be the source of our joy forever.
Of this verse; [g: non-perception of both]. || 1 ||
Her ears adorned with golden, swaying earrings; her breasts full and firm; decorated with ornaments of pearl necklaces; with jasmine flowers shining within her elegantly braided hair;
her eyes rolling with playful charm; moon-faced; and wearing a girdle-strand fastened around her waist.
We daily salute the Mother, the Sovereign of the World, who sports [in her divine play]. || 2 ||

Now, for those virtuous ones who are agitated by the waves of the great ocean of wretchedness and the like, and who are as difficult to fathom as the swirling circle of the crocodiles of all the sense-faculties— just like the earring of a sea-monster—

Having attained the grace of her who is like a true boat for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra— so difficult to fathom and filled with the great delusion that incessantly increases— and who is the abode of all prosperity;
Even the four-faced Brahmā, at the beginning of creation, instantly caused to sprout all the sciences proclaimed in the entirety of the Vedas and Āgamas—
namely the fourteen branches of knowledge—
just as one does for the lotus-navelled Viṣṇu.

Like a mother, she was intent on providing care; like a wish-fulfilling creeper, she was skilled in bestowing desired fruits; and by the treading of her beautiful feet, she seemed to support the earth with compassion.
[She who seemed to be providing protection,] with jeweled anklets jingling at her feet.

Adorned with all foot-ornaments such as jeweled anklets jingling at her feet; resounding with the tinkling of a multitude of small bells on a shimmering, excellent girdle; and possessing a smooth [gait].
Appearing like a reflection in water that does not remain still [variant: appearing like a drop of water resting on the edge of a *pippala* leaf; variant: appearing slippery...].

Her full and elevated breasts were adorned with necklaces of strings of pure pearls; her beautiful golden earrings reflected the pair of pigeons with sweet warbling that mirrored the reflection of her hands, feet, and cheeks, which surpassed the splendor of fresh *madhuka* flowers.

Having saluted the Mistress of the World (Bhuvaneśī), who is resplendent with the great ruby of her crown shimmering as it is reflected in the pair of her excellent cheeks— which surpasses a cluster of nine bandhūka flowers— and whose beautiful eyebrows are mirrored therein.

The commentator, Paḍmanābha Paṇḍita, makes this declaration: "I shall compose a commentary on the *Mahāstotra* composed by the sovereign of all masters of the Āgamas, the teacher Pṛthvīdhara— a commentary that illuminates every pure word and serves as an awakening for the ignorant, according to my own capacity."

O Mother, I meditate upon that supreme form of Yours, which consists of the pervasive resonance (*nāda*), whose head is adorned with the digit of the moon (*aindavī kalā*), and which is the one absolute Reality (*sanmātra*);
therein arises the venerable Goddess known as Parā, who is indeed the ground of all those manifestations.
The Paśyantī and the Madhyamā abide [within], and that Vaikharī moves at its own will.

It is one whose head is adorned—that is, whose head and crown is made into a crest—by what? By the lunar—that is, by the digit belonging to the moon. By a digit (*kalā*) related to the *Indu* (the Moon). Furthermore, of what nature is your form?

It is "expansive" (*vistāri*), meaning it possesses expansion; that is to say, it is all-pervading. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is "consisting of resonance" (*nādātmaka*)—at the time of utterance, it is like a resonance (*nāda*), being pure existence (*sanmātra*).
Its nature is sound (*nāda*), like that which possesses sound at the time of utterance. Furthermore, what is it like? It is "supreme" (*parama*);
that whose splendor (*mā*) is supreme—that is, most excellent—is the meaning of "supreme," meaning preeminent. Furthermore, what is it like? It is pure being (*sanmātra*).

That is to say, it is of the nature of pure existence. Furthermore, of what kind is it? It is one, without a second. O Viśveśvarī (O Mother), in which form of yours the supreme designation—the word "Parā"—arises, that is, attains its manifestation; what kind of word is that? It is the Blessed Goddess herself.

She possesses the sixfold sovereignty and knowledge; for it is heard in various senses that "Bhaga" means the sun, "Orka" means light, and "Jñāna" means knowledge—as seen in the observation of these manifold meanings.
Furthermore, what kind of supreme designation is there? For that is certainly the locus of those very sounds;
it is the established locus, the place of those renowned sounds and illuminations. From that, the supreme designation, the *paśyantī* speech, manifests;
following after that *paśyantī*, the *madhyamā* speech subsequently manifests, and from that, [the *vaikharī*] manifests at will.

And by her own will, that speech—well-known as *vaikharī*, which has been made manifest in eight locations—sports forth. Furthermore, in the context of Manu, the phrase "his head adorned with the lunar digit" (*aiṃdavyā kalayāvataṃsitaśiro*) is observed to be written as an imitation of the crescent moon. Thereafter...
That from which extensive proliferation (*prapañca*) arises is *māyā*; therefore, the extracted meaning is "the seed of *māyā* that is extensive.
Following that, it is "of the nature of *nāda*"; here, by the word *nāda*, the *bindu* (anusvāra) is denoted, and thus it means "accompanied by that," i.e., with the anusvāra, namely *hrīṃ*.
Now, revealing the extraordinary majesty of Vaikharī, he speaks the subsequent verse:

"But that fourth [power], consisting of the sciences beginning with the Vedas, which triumphs having embraced the three worlds through its longing for the playful manifestation of the letters from 'A' to 'Kṣa'— [of those powers, it is the fourth]."

Grant me grace regarding that speech, which bestows the attainment of the sovereignty of poetry—a state so praiseworthy that it consists in listening to and describing the tumultuous play of the waves of nectar. || 2 ||

"Ādi"—O Mother, Sovereign of All! The word "tu" (but) serves as a delimiter; among those aforementioned modes of speech characterized as Parā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī, the fourth—namely Vaikharī—is that which, having embraced the triple world (*jagattraya*), the three realms of existence, [the triad].

It triumphs by pervading, that is, it exists with supreme excellence. By what means? By the intense longing for the play of the letters from *ā* to *kṣa*. "From *ā*" refers to the vowels beginning with *a*; "ending with *kṣa*" refers to those phonemes ending with the letter *kṣa*. Their "play" is their manifestation; the "intense longing" for that is a specific mode of pronunciation. By that [mode], it triumphs.

The meaning is that she exists pervading the entire universe due to her eager delight in the play of the letters from *a* to *kṣa*. Of what nature is that fourth (*turīyā*) Vaikharī? She is composed of the sciences beginning with the Vedas—that is, she whose essential form consists of those sciences such as the Vedas.
O Mother, [worship] that fourth Vaikharī [which is characterized by the Vaikharī speech].
Grant full grace to my speech; having established perfect serenity, bring it forth. What kind of speech?
One that bestows the attainment of the empire of poetry, which is worthy of description upon hearing the tumultuous play of its waves of nectar.
Of what is this nectar? It is the sweet sound—the clamor—of those very waves, the surges of ambrosia. Its...

"Play" (krīḍā) means sporting; the hearing of that is what is to be described. That which is praiseworthy poetry, the attainment of sovereignty therein—which is the accomplishment of moving about according to one's own will—is that which "bestows" (prakarṣeṇa dadāti) such a perfection; thus she is so described. (2)
4) Now, he describes the majesty of the distinguished Vāgbhava [syllable]: "At the beginning of the Kalpa, even the Lotus-seated One (Brahmā) was indeed pierced by some part [of it]."
Having meditated upon you, he caused the four Vedas and those various sciences to sprout forth.
O Mother Lalitā, be gracious; grant me a straightforward eloquence of Sarasvatī, at the fragrance of which the deities dwelling within him manifest through horripilation. (3)
"At the beginning of the eon"—O Mother, O Janani, "indeed" (kila) means truly;

at the beginning of the eon, that is, at the start of creation, even the Lotus-Seated One, Brahmā himself, having meditated upon you, caused the four Vedas and those ten sciences to sprout—that is, he manifested them. Of what nature was the Lotus-Seated One? Even he.
"By what certain part has he been pierced and sewn together? Furthermore, how is he clever?"—this is an epithet of Brahmā.

O Mother, for that reason, be gracious; show favor to me and grant me simple eloquence (*sārasvatam*). [The word *saralam* is derived from] *sa*, *ra*, and *la*; and according to the rule "every *dvandva* compound may optionally be singular," it is treated as a single unit.

The meaning is: "accompanied by these syllables," or alternatively, "straight" (*saralam*) means "upright" (*prāñjalam*), that is, consisting solely of the *vāgbhava* in the form of the syllable *aiṃ*. O Lalitā, the prayer is: "Extend this mantra, which is the *vāgbhava* and possesses such majesty, within me. Furthermore, O Viśveśvarī, [the prayer continues: "of whom the fragrance of the *vāgbhava*... [Kh: for me...]

Grant me the *sārasvata* [mantra], which is straightforward and distinguished by qualities such as the sweetness of understanding its meaning, and not marred by irregularities or the like— that *vāgbhava* whose fragrance causes the deities residing within to manifest through horripilation;
that is, the fragrance and majesty of which, abiding within the heart, are the deities beginning with the Self (*ātman*).
They cause [it] to arise by means of what? By means of *pulakas*, that is to say, by means of horripilation (*romāñcas*). || 3 ||
Now, he describes the fruit of meditating on another seed-syllable of the Bhagavatī:
"O Mother! For those who bear bodies, you are composed of fortitude, consisting solely of the line of *nāda*, composed of *prāṇa*, composed of fire, and established in the *bindu*."
Therefore, I meditate upon you, the victorious Mistress of the World, as the Consort of the All-pervading Lord;
may my well-spoken verses, their minds purified by the blossoming of your compassion, sport in delight. || 4 ||
"O Mother"— the word "aho" is used here as an address— O Mother,
you exist in such a manner (of the characteristics to be described) for those who bear bodies, that is, for embodied beings; for that reason,
[you are] the wife and the mistress of the all-pervading Mahādeva.

I meditate upon Bhuvaneśvarī. Of what nature are you? You are victorious, possessing the quality of victory; therefore, may my *sūktayas*—my beautiful words—sport in the endeavor of composing ever-new prose and verse (the meaning is: may my ever-new compositions consisting of prose and verse shine forth).

May [those whose minds are purified by merit through the blossoming of compassion] shine forth, exerting themselves in the immediate composition of ever-new prose and verse. Of what nature are these utterances?
[They are those whose minds are meritorious and expanded by compassion.
Those whose minds are thus—expanded by your compassion (*tvatkāruṇya*), radiant through your mercy (*tvatkaruṇā*), luminous in nature, opening wide, meritorious, and pure; and what are you like?
You are composed of steadfastness (*dhṛti*).
Dhṛti consists of the letter *ī* and is composed of that; furthermore, what are you like?
You consist of a single line of *nāda*. Here, by the word *nāda*, the letter *u* is understood—its single line is the digit of the moon (*candrakalā*), and you are composed of that.

Furthermore, what is its nature? It is *prāṇamayī* (composed of breath); *prāṇa* is the letter *ha*, and it consists of that. Furthermore, what is its nature? It is *hutāśanamayī* (composed of fire); *hutāśana* is the letter *ra*, and it consists of that. Furthermore, what is its nature? It is *bindupratiṣṭhāmayī* (composed of the foundation of the *bindu*);
the *bindu* is the *anusvāra*, and its *pratiṣṭhā* is its placement; it consists of that. Thus, *hrīṃ* becomes the mantra. Here.

In all the qualifiers beginning with "consisting of fortitude" (dhṛtimayī), the application of the suffix *mayaṭ*— which signifies the meaning of essential nature— is intended to indicate that she is composed of each respective quality.
Now, he describes the construction of the yantra:
"I daily worship that very Goddess of Speech, the Mistress of the World (Bhuvaneśvarī), who resembles a leaf of the holy fig tree (aśvattha), who is sweet, and whose belly is bound by a support."

May my divine words play— words that have conquered the playful movement of the waves of spontaneous awakening in the ocean of nectar, and which possess the fragrance of intimacy with the autumnal moonlight. || 5 ||

"Tvām iti"—O Mother! day after day (*anudinaṃ dinaṃ dinaṃ*), having made her my constant object of focus, I worship and properly propitiate you, that very Goddess of Speech who is the Sovereign of the World (*bhuvaneśvarī*). For that reason, may my divine words and voices shine forth.

Let them play. Of what nature are these words? They surpass the playful movement of the waves of the nectar-ocean, which rises from its familiarity with the fragrance accompanying the autumnal moonlight (*śāradakaumudī*). Here, [the compound] *śāradakaumudī* is formed as "that which belongs to autumn" (*śāradī*) and is also "moonlight" (*kaumudī*), thus "autumnal moonlight. In this case, [the feminine suffix] *striyāḥ* [is applied].

By the rule *puṃvadbhāṣitapuṃskāt*, there is a masculine transformation (*puṃvadbhāva*) of the preceding member, resulting in its elision. This is its acquaintance or observation; by that, the ocean of nectar—the sea of ambrosia—becomes surging and overflowing.

[She is] "conquering" (jayantī) that playful grace (vibhrama) which belongs to those waves (vīcayaḥ)—that is, ripples—that are noisy and wakeful at will (svairaṃ svecchayā). Of what nature are you? You are "sweet in the imitation of an *aśvattha* leaf," meaning by way of resembling the leaf of the holy fig tree (*pippala*).

"Sweet" means sweet with its three corners [kh: "charming"; g: "charming by means of the triangle"]. "With a belly bound by the foundation" means having its interior bound by the hexagon at the foundation (ādhāra), thus constructed as a dwelling; by this much, previously—
Having drawn a triangle (p.
and then having fashioned a hexagon after that, subsequently, for the duration of eight watches of the day...

Because it consists of eight watches (prahara), it is conventionally designated as an "eight-petaled lotus. Then, one should inscribe in its center the seed-syllable of speech (*vāṅmaya*), accompanied by the crescent moon and the nasal bindu; such is the procedure for the extraction of the yantra. || 5 ||
Now, he describes the meditation upon the Supreme Sovereign (Parameśvarī):
O Mother, may your beautiful left hand— adorned with a book of radiant splendor, fragrant with the objects of knowledge presented by the scribe, and bestowing well-being— be auspicious for me.
May that other finger as well— dense with a mass of straightness like a cluster of coral sprouts and bearing the seal consisting of pure awakening— remain forever free from delusion.
*Lekheti*—O Mother, may your left hand be a bringer of well-being (*svastikṛt*) and a maker of auspiciousness for me. Of what nature is that left hand?
It is joined with a book, the crest-jewel of glorious splendor, fragrant with the objects of knowledge presented by writing; that is, the objects of knowledge which are presented by means of writing.

The book, which elucidates the subject matter currently under discussion— that is, the object to be known— and which is adorned with a crest consisting of its captivating splendor, namely the beauty of its fragrant fragrance, is thus decorated.
Furthermore, what is he like? He is "abhirāma" with "śrī," meaning captivating with beauty.

His other right hand—may it immediately, at that very moment, be one whose delusion is cast away (*apāstabhrama*), meaning its error is dispelled. What is it doing? [It is] bestowing knowledge (*bodha*).

Bearing a mudrā; furthermore, of what nature is he? One whose fingers are dense with the mass of straightness—the graceful, upright beauty—of the coral-creeper (vidrumakandalī). [According to manuscript *kh*: "Dense" means his fingers are joined together by that graceful, upright beauty.]
"He whose fingers [are thus]"—this is an adjective qualifying both [the subject and the object]. || 6 ||
Then, seeking with a glance of compassionate grace from the Blessed Lady, he says:
"O Mother, your glances are hardened by the sport of uprooting the entire web of sins."
May your perfected powers, tender with the nectar of compassion, manifest within me; through these,

I shall produce an outpouring of qualities worthy of the Four-faced One (Brahmā), whose mind is not bewildered by the eager curiosity and intentional play of the waves of this composition intended for his own pleasure.
[He spoke] these words. || 7 ||

"O Mother"—O Mother, may your glances flash and shine upon me, your object of affection; what kind of glances? Those which are hardened by the sport of uprooting the very foundation of the web of sins—that is, the mass of sins, its root being the bulbous root, and [hardened] by the playful act of burning or tearing it away.

Furthermore, how are those who are harsh by nature? They are tender with the nectar of compassion; "compassion" (kāruṇya) means pity (karuṇā), and that itself is the nectar (amṛta)—[in the Kha and G manuscripts, "pīyūṣa"]—by which they are tender (komalāḥ) [in the Kha and G manuscripts, "mṛdulāḥ"]. Furthermore, they are strengthened by spiritual perfection (siddhi); [in the Kha and G manuscripts, "by yours"].
"By means of this propitiation, being empowered and impelled, O Sureśvarī, with these very eyes I shall produce speech; that is, I shall manifest my voice.
What kind of speech?

[The compound is: *svābhimataprabandhalaharīsākūtakautūhalābhrāntasvāntacaturmukhocita-* [kh; g: consisting of prose, verse, and so forth]. Of that [work], there is a "wave" (*laharī*), which is its manifestation; the "significant curiosity" (*sākūtakautūhala*) is the interest accompanied by intentional meaning; therein, the mind is "bewildered" (*ābhrānta*)—[g: "overwhelmed" (*ākrānta*)].

"Śliṣṭam" means pure; that internal mind (svānta) which is such—by it, she is "tathā," meaning one in whom there is an outpouring (udgāra)—that is, a manifestation—of qualities (guṇas) that is appropriate (ucita), resembling that of the Four-faced One, Brahmā. || 7 ||
Now he describes the procedure for the worship of the Bhagavatī:
"I worship you, who reside within the four-petalled lotus of the Ādhāra, in the womb of the seed-syllable Vāgbīja,
as the lofty creeper of Māyā, blossoming through the successive invocations beginning with the first."

It is world-transcending, possessing the singular wonder of the circular movement of its churning wheel, which is agitated by waves of nectar swaying and sporting upon the lotuses that serve as the sacred leaves at the base of its crest.

"Tvām iti"—O Mother! I worship you, the creeper of Māyā (the *hrīṃ* syllable), within the womb of the seed-syllable of Speech (*vāgbīja*), namely, in the center of the *aiṃ* syllable. Of what nature is this creeper of Māyā? It resides upon the four-petalled lotus of the Ādhāra; that is, the Ādhāra-cakra itself is the four-petalled lotus, a lotus with four petals.

Furthermore, what is she like when she has gone there and is standing? She is "elevated" (*unnatā*). Furthermore, what is she like? She is "in bloom" (*kusumitā*), that is, flowering, with the initial letters beginning with *a* and so forth. For other creepers also, being elevated, become flowering. With what kind of initial letters?
By "pratyāvṛttibhiḥ": those whose existence or operation (*vṛtti*) is directed toward each one individually and on all sides are *pratyāvṛttayaḥ*;

by them, thus. Alternatively, by the *pratyāvṛttis*, that is, the letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa', which are in direct and reverse order, [the city] was made to blossom (*kusumitām*).

The meaning is "endowed with supreme beauty. Just as *hrīṃ aṃ hrīṃ āṃ* and so forth, the letters ending with *kṣa* (or *sa*, according to manuscript *kh*) are to be inferred by oneself. In reverse order, for example:
*hrīṃ kṣaṃ hrīṃ laṃ hrīṃ saṃ*, and so on. Furthermore, of what nature is this *māyā-latā*?

That which is agitated by the surging waves of nectar— the waves of ambrosia playing with extreme restlessness within the "lotus of the sacred leaf" at the crown of the head (brahmarandhra)— that lotus of the sacred leaf being a stainless thousand-petaled lotus where the nectar-waves sport in a swaying dance.

Because it has the form of a wheel (*cakra*), it is a "wheel" (*cakram*), which is a collection of petals; by means of the wonder of its movement (*caṅkrama*) and the wonder of its appearance (*vilokana*), it is supramundane and ineffable. || 8 ||
Now, he describes the fruit resulting from the propitiation of the Supreme Sovereign (Parameśvarī):

"Thus, taking refuge in the compassionate side-glance of Your Majesty, I withdraw my mind from its wandering through the five paths and dwell [in meditation]; may my tongue embrace the stage of the aesthetic delight."

The Goddess of Speech possesses a beauty like the dense waters of the crystal mountain Sphaṭikādri, flowing freely as the nectar streaming from the artistic effusions created by the illustrious Sarvajñavibhūṣaṇa. 9.

"O Mother, I am that very person—your servant; taking refuge in the glance of your compassionate eye, and taking refuge in the sight of your merciful side-long look, I dwell and remain here. Having done what? Having withdrawn (turned back) the mind, the consciousness—from what?"
Because of the movement through the five paths of all five winds, beginning with prāṇa, due to the movement of the five paths of [the winds] which are the selves,
and because of the transition across the five paths; and wherever there is the movement of the wind, there is the mind.

Its movement is also heard of; or else, through the movement— that is, the circulation— of the five paths (adhvan), namely the Gāṇapatya, Vaiṣṇava, Saura, Śāktika, and Śāmbhava, the mind (manas) [becomes] established in the vital breath (vāyu).
Since I dwell in you alone after having brought this about, for that reason let Bhāratī—the tongue of the gods—embrace and take refuge in the stage. Of what nature is Bhāratī?
She who flows from the crystal mountain of her own free will, which is the overflowing nectar of the arts adorned by the illustrious Omniscient One.

The illustrious omniscient Maheśa— whose crescent moon serves as his ornament— from that [crescent] flows forth the nectar and ambrosia; and that which is the independent, supportless, and stainless Crystal Mountain (Sphaṭikādri)— [the nectar] is condensed by those two.

It is so called because it possesses a splendor (*bhā*) exactly like that which arises when milk (*payas*) and curd (*dugdha*) are mixed together in abundance; or else, because of the nectar flowing from the digit of the moon (*candrakalā*), which serves as an ornament for the Great Lord (*maheśvara*), the Omniscient One (*sarvajña*).
This meaning is appropriate: she possesses a splendor like that of the water which has been thickened—that is, made abundant—of the mountain of clear crystal, a mountain of spotless crystal;
for the moonbeams rain down nectar. (Because the moonbeams rain down nectar...)
By the sight of that [sun], the crystal mountain melts; those two, having become one, shine in that manner—such is the summarized meaning of "tadvat seti" (it shines like that). || 9 ||

9) Now he describes another method for the recitation of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the Bhagavatī: "O Mother! This [seed-syllable] is interwoven with the Mātṛkā and contains the Unstruck Sound (*anāhata*) within its womb."

Obeisance to Your splendor, which consists of Māyā and is delightful like an ocean of self-dependent nectar; it delights in the path that is to be drunk through the resonance of Svachchanda, and on the mountain where the moon and sun sleep, it is served by the upward movement of the phonemes starting from 'A', arranged in the method of reversal. 10.

"O Mother"—the word "aho" is used here as an address—O Mother, I thoroughly worship (or, according to manuscript *g*, meditate upon) this great light of yours consisting of *māyā*. Of what nature is this great light consisting of *māyā*? It is that which is to be drunk as the unstruck (*anāhata*) spontaneous sound (*svacchanda-dhvani*) contained within it. Regarding the term "contained" (*garbhīkṛta*): that which was not a womb (*agarbha*) has become a womb (*garbha*).

"Made" (*kṛtaḥ*) means contained within; that which is the sound of the unstruck (*anāhata-dhvani*), the unstruck (*anāhata*) produced by its own will—that by which the drinkable and the visible are [perceived]. Furthermore, what is it like?
Consisting of illusion (*māyāmaya*), it is delighted on the path of the mountain of the sleep of the moon and sun;

being free from the activity of sleep during the inhalation and exhalation of the moon and sun, it is like a mountain— that mountain of the sleep of the moon and sun— on which very path, in the *svādhiṣṭhāna-cakra*, it is again delighted, that is, established.
Of what nature is this great splendor consisting of illusion? It is interlaced with the *mātṛkā* and woven together with the *mātṛkā*, such as:
*aiṃ hrīṃ aṃ aiṃ hrīṃ āṃ*, and so forth, up to *kṣa*; this is how it should be understood.
Furthermore, of what nature is that illusory glory (*māyāmayaṃ mahaḥ*)? It is "charming like the ocean of nectar under its own control" (*svādhīnāmṛtasiṃdhubaṃdhuraṃ*);
that is to say, it is as enchanting as the ocean of nectar which is under its own control—that is, subject to its own will—and thus bestows desired fruits. Again, how is it qualified?

From the utterance of the matrix (mātṛkā) of the inverted arrangement of the sequence, up to the letter *a*: that is, from the utterance of the matrix of the inverted arrangement of the sequence, up to the letter *a*, as follows: *aiṃ hrīṃ kṣaṃ aiṃ hrīṃ haṃ aiṃ hrīṃ yaṃ*.

Aiṃ hrīṃ kṣaṃ, aiṃ hrīṃ haṃ, aiṃ hrīṃ saṃ, aiṃ hrīṃ ṣaṃ, hrīṃ śaṃ—one should infer for oneself [the sequence] up to the letter *a*; one should infer for oneself [the sequence] up to the letter *a*. || 10 ||
Now, he describes the fruit that arises from the worship of the seed-syllable (bīja) of the Supreme Goddess:
"Therefore, [the fruit belongs] to those women with unrestrained brows, whose minds rejoice in the free indulgence in flower-liquor under the shade of beautiful sandal trees in the Nandana grove."
Grant me here that ever-flowing Sarasvata speech by which even the wondrous charm of sounds, rippling like the waves of a lute, may become devoid of essence.
"Therefore"—O Mother, therefore, from the service of your splendor (*mahaḥ*), grant and bestow upon me in this world the Sarasvata [speech]; of what nature? Abounding on all sides (*abhitaḥ*).
Even though it is mobile and has the nature of spreading everywhere,
by which Sarasvata [speech] would one certainly become devoid of essence, deprived of vitality, and rendered tasteless? Who is that?
The wonder of the notes, rippling with the melodic modulations of the lute: the lute is well known; its "modulation" (bhaṅgi) refers to a particular arrangement of the strings;

by that modulation, the "rippling" (taraṅgita)—meaning resonated, raised up, or produced—refers to the wonder, the enchanting effect, of the notes such as *niṣāda* and the rest; that is the sentiment of the Heroic (*vīrarasa*).
Such is the connection: of which [women]? Of those unrestrained women with beautiful brows, who are as lovely as the celestial damsels of the gods;

of what characteristics? Of those women whose minds rejoice in freely tasting the floral intoxicants beneath the shade of the beautiful sandalwood trees in the Nandana grove—those beautiful sandalwood trees that are in the Nandana forest.

Those women whose minds were thus filled with joy and delight by the free and spontaneous tasting of the nectar— the essence of flowers— from those captivating sandalwood trees in their shade. || 11 ||

Now, with a verse to be spoken by the Blessed Lady, he states the locations for the three seed-syllables—[according to manuscript *kh*: he states the meditation; according to manuscript *g*: he states the locations for the meditation on the three seed-syllables]:
"Having fixed the intellect consisting of wisdom upon the foundation, the heart, and the region of the crest..."

O Mother, as I chant your name— threefold in form, the slender essence of the seed-syllables, and a wave of the nectar of non-deficient compassion— may my limbs thrill with horripilation through mouthfuls of the water of wisdom that tastes the unimpeded nectar of one’s own non-duality. 12.

Regarding the word "ādhāra" (the support): O Mother, as I recite the seed-principle (*bījatattva*) that is you, may my limbs—the parts of my body—become elevated, swelling up and throbbing with what? With horripilation (*pulaka*), the bristling of the hair. Having done what? Having [placed] the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) which will be mentioned in the following verse within these [limbs].
Having joined together in three ways at three places—having established a threefold connection—at which places?
At the lower [place], the *ādhāra-cakra*; at the heart; at the mind (*mānasa*); at the vicinity of the crest-lock (*śikhā*); and at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
With what kind of thrills (*pulaka*)? [Kh: having brought them into proximity.]

With handfuls of the water of wisdom—the water of knowledge consisting of the unrestrained, limitless tasting of the nectar of one's own non-duality—I [worship you]. What kind of you? You who are composed of *medhā* (intellectual power), whose very nature is *medhā*. [Note on the compound: "Unrestrained" (*niraṅkuśa*) means devoid of limits (*maryādā-rahitam*). "The tasting of the nectar of one's own non-duality" (*nijasya... advaitāmṛtāsvādanam*) refers to the experience of the non-dual self. "The water of wisdom" (*prajñāmbhas*) is the water of gnosis (*jñāna-jalam*). "With handfuls" (*culukaiḥ*) refers to the scoops of that water. What is her form? She is of the nature of *medhā*.

Furthermore, of what nature is she? She is one in whom there exist waves and surges of the nectar of compassion (*karuṇāpīyūṣa*)—that is, the ambrosia of mercy—which is "not deficient" (*anūna*), meaning it is constant and abundant. Thus she is described as such. (Alternatively: she is a river of waves consisting of that nectar of compassion.)
The meaning is "Taraṅgavatī. || 12 ||
Now, he describes the fruit of meditating upon the three seed-syllables:

"O Mother, I mutter this supreme seed-syllable of Speech known as Kāmarāja, which is followed by the letter *sa*, joined with the visarga, and preceded by the vowel *u*; by that [may my desires be fulfilled]."
May this wondrous speech, whose essence has been drunk by the steadfast ones who have begun the lustration ceremony with jewels fixed in their long-swaying crests, expand incessantly. (13)

Regarding the word *vāṇī*: O Mother, Sovereign of All (or, according to manuscript G, Sovereign of the Whole), for that reason, may this wondrous speech of mine blossom and flow forth incessantly and perpetually.
For what reason? Because I recite this seed-syllable of speech (*vāṇībīja*), which is the form of the syllable *aiṃ*, in the *ādhāra-cakra*. Furthermore than that...

I recite the Kāmarāja mantra in the form of the syllable *klīṃ* at my heart. Then, it is "sāntapara": that which has the letter *sa* as its end (*anta*) and is followed by the supreme (*para*). Furthermore, what is it like? It is that which is accompanied by the *visarga* and follows the diphthong *au*. That is, it is joined with the *visarga* and has the vowel *au* as its subsequent part.
Following the letter *u* together with the *visarga*, the seed-syllable of Śakti, *sauṃ*— as in *sauriti* according to manuscript *kh*—

I recite through the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) alone; or else, when the placement of a specific seed-syllable is performed in the phrase "ending in *sa* and supreme" (*sāntaparam*), it is indeed thus that the construction of the compound is formed.
The formation of the compound: here, by the word *anta*, the letter *ha* is obtained because it is associated with the letter *sa*. Thus, the letter *sa* follows the letter *ha*;

that seed-syllable (*bīja*) which has something following the letter *ha* at its end is "that which has *sa* after the end" (*sāntaparam*). This is the form *hsauṃ*, the seed-syllable of Śakti. What kind of speech is this?

By which wise ones was the juice drunk? By which wise ones was the flavor tasted? By those steadfast ones who had commenced the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) with jewels set in their turbans that were swayed for a long time—those by whom jewels were fixed and placed in turbans that were swayed as far as possible, and by whom the lustration was begun with those very [jewels].

Likewise by them. Of what nature is the triad of seeds? It is "supreme" (*parama*), meaning that which possesses supreme (*parama*) beauty (*mā*); or alternatively, it is "supreme" because it possesses the beauty of *parā*, that is, the speech (*vāṇī*) designated as *parā*. Thus, it is indeed an epithet of the seed-syllables of speech. || 13 ||
Now, he describes the meditation on the Blessed Lady’s fruitful right arm:
She who bears, with great intensity, a rosary bracelet that is worthy of being mistaken for a cluster of nectar-drops trickling incessantly from the digit of the moon upon her crest.
O Mother, you are yourself reciting your own mantra within the mind, with syllables manifest through direct perception;
therefore, with your right hand, bestow upon me abundant blessings.

"Cūḍā" means: O Mother! You, who are of the form described above, bestow—that is, produce—abundant blessings for me with your right hand (the specific reading "me" meaning "for me" is found in manuscript *kh*).
You, who are exceedingly beautiful and composed of crystal gems... [manuscript *kh*].

Wearing a rosary of beads made of crystal-like gems, you, being virtuous, recite within yourself your own mantra consisting of syllables; what kind of syllable? One that functions perceptibly, directed toward each and every *akṣa*.
That whose function (*vṛtti*) or operation (*vartana*) is such is "of that nature. Alternatively, that whose function is perceptible (*pratyakṣa*) is "perceptible-functioned" (*pratyakṣavṛtti*).
Of what kind is this bracelet of rosary beads?

"Worthy of doubt through the beauty of dripping drops of nectar": by means of the splendor (*śrī*) of those drops of nectar (*pīyūṣabindu*) which drip continuously— that is, without interruption— from the digit of the moon (*candrakalā*) that has become her crest-ornament (*śekharībhūtā*), it is "worthy of doubt" (*sandehocitam*).
Because it is exceedingly white, the meaning is that it has a form corresponding to and resembling that [light]. || 14 ||
Now, he describes the meditation on the left arm of the Blessed Lady:
Having assumed the *svastika* posture, which is ever-beautiful with rows of skin as pure as the breaking of white light,
while she is perpetually yawning amidst blooming lotuses...
I constantly worship the Goddess of Speech, who, while her arm is gracefully extended, rests her beautiful hand upon her left knee as she plays, and who is ever devoted to holding a book. 15.

"Having bound"—I constantly and uninterruptedly worship and propitiate the Mistress of Speech (*girām īśvarīm*), who is the presiding deity of words (*vācām adhidevatām*); how is she? The Mistress of Speech, who is fond of holding a book in her hand—that is, in her paw.

"She who has a longing—that is, an affection—for holding a book, her [is described as such]. With what kind of hand? One placed beautifully upon the left knee, having been set there. Having done what? Having assumed the *svastika* posture—the seat known by that name. Of what nature is that posture?"
The beauty of the fortune of the pure luster of the fragments of white light—that which is the fragment (*cheda*), the breaking (*bhaṅga*), of the moon (*sitaruci*) or of crystal and the like;
its pure luster (*avadātacchavi*) is its brilliance (*ujjvalatā*); the series (*śreṇī*) of that [brilliance]; of that [series]... which...

[She is] Śrī, beauty; by that, she is *subhaga*, captivating. Furthermore, what is her nature? She is *bhaviṣṇu*, having the habit of becoming [manifest]. Again, what is the nature of her speech? It is *īśvarī*, sovereign. She is constantly playing (*adhidīvyantī*) upon the blooming lotuses, endowed with exceeding splendor (*adhika-śobhā-yuktām*). [Kh: ...endowed with that...]
[This is] appropriate. || 15 ||
Now, he describes the distinguished fruit of meditation upon the Blessed Lady [the Supreme Sovereign]:
"That [speech] of mine, which traverses all paths, thick, shimmering, and boundless Sarasvatī..."
May this eloquence of mine, beautiful with its various shifting ripples like the currents of a river,
shine forth— listening to which the wise, their minds reeling,
would despise even a digit of the moon with their heads swaying and the corners of their eyes closing. (16)
p.
12) *tanme iti*—O Mother, from such meditation upon you as this, may my speech (*bhāratī*) shine forth—that is, may it be beautiful. Of what nature is it?
The Goddess of Speech (Bhāratī) is beautiful with the various, charming, and playful waves of the boundless stream of Sarasvatī;

"pervading all paths" (*viśvapathīna*) means that which extends across every path—that is, all-pervasive—and "pīna" means mature or full, while "vilasat" means endowed with playfulness, and "nissīma" means limitless or without boundary; this is the stream belonging to Sarasvatī (*sārasvata*).

The stream of its waves consists of various beautiful and charming modulations; hearing such speech, even the wise ones—the gods or scholars—would find fault with a digit of the moon. Of what nature are these wise ones?

Those whose minds were reeling—meaning those whose minds were whirling—[which are] likewise delightful and joy-inducing; furthermore, by what? By the corners of their eyes closing; and by what else? By means of their heads, that is, their crowns; of what nature were they? They were swaying.
"By those who have shaken" means by those who have tossed or agitated them. || 16 ||
Now, he describes another method for the recitation (*japa*) of the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the Supreme Goddess:

"First the Vāgbhava [syllable], sweet with the moon and the bindu; at the end of *jhā* and the end of *yoga*, the one consisting of desire (*kāma*); and the third between *ka* and *ṣa*: meditating thus upon those three seed-syllables..."

O Maheśvarī, having joined the Mātṛkā in reverse and in an irregular manner, and by means of the speech that severs the bonds which resides within, one hundred measures (mātrā) are recited by me. || 17 ||

Regarding the word "at first" (*ādau*): O Mother! O Maheśvarī! A hundred repetitions of the *mātrās* are chanted by me with internal speech. By what means? In this manner: having joined and bound the three seed-syllables together with the *mātṛkā* in such a way that they become reversed and irregular, while meditating—that is, contemplating—what [is done] at the beginning?

At the beginning of the letter *a*, there is the seed-syllable of Speech (*vāgbhava*), namely *aiṃ*, which is sweet with the moon-drop—the moon being a digit of the moon and the drop being the *anusvāra*—and thus charming by means of these two, or accompanied by them; furthermore, at the end of the letter *jha*, there is the syllable *klīṃ*, whose nature is desire. After that...

At the end of the conjunction of the two *kaṣas* (the letters *kṣ*), at the end of the letter *kṣa*, is the third seed-syllable of Śakti, namely *sauḥ*. It is as follows: *aiṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ klīṃ ñaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ taṃ thaṃ*.

daṃ dhaṃ naṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ sauṃḥ | In reverse order, as follows: sauṃḥ kṣaṃ laṃ haṃ ṣaṃ śaṃ vaṃ laṃ raṃ yaṃ maṃ bhaṃ baṃ phaṃ paṃ naṃ dhaṃ daṃ thaṃ taṃ ṇaṃ ḍhaṃ ḍaṃ ṭhaṃ.

Ṭaṃ ñaṃ klīṃ jhaṃ jaṃ chaṃ caṃ ṅaṃ ghaṃ gaṃ khaṃ kaṃ aṃḥ aṃ auṃ oṃ aiṃ eṃ ḹṃ ḷṃ ṝṃ ṛṃ ūṃ uṃ īṃ iṃ āṃ aṃ aiṃ. Furthermore, by me who am what? By me, the "severer of bonds" (*bandhacchid*); "bond" (*bandha*) refers to *saṃsāra*, and because I sever that, I am the "severer of bonds. Thus [is it]. 17.
14) Now he states the fruit of propitiating the Bhagavatī: "May that sovereign status of Sarasvatī shine forth for me immediately."

Where even the collection of the fifth musical note (*pañcama*), which is honored by the descent of the warbling of cuckoos awakened by the month of Caitra, is sprinkled with praise as it kisses speech made abundant by hundreds of great poets who have acted according to his command.
It is like a cloud. || 18 ||

Regarding the word "tat": O Mother! for that reason, may my status as a sovereign of Sarasvatī shine forth at once—that is, at this very moment—certainly in that sovereign status where speech [shines].

For men who kiss and listen to such speech, even a mere collection of sounds would be like a burden; for what is this? It is the praise adorned by the descent of the "kuhū" warbling of the playful cuckoos awakened by Caitra.
The male cuckoos have their descent into the sound *kuhū*; by means of that, the praise and eulogy which is obtained and reached becomes augmented and increased,
yet even that collection of the fifth musical note (*pañcama-śruti*) becomes like a burden.
What kind of speech? One expanded and perfected by hundreds of great poets.

By what kind of hundreds of great poets? By those acting according to their command (*ājñāvihita*). This "command" refers to the rule in great compositions—that is, in meters such as the *āryā*—wherein wherever a heavy syllable (*guru*) is observed, there must be a heavy syllable alone, and wherever a light syllable (*laghu*) is observed, there must be a light syllable alone.
They were enjoined and impelled by them. || 18 ||
Now he describes another meditation involving the mantra of the Bhagavatī:
having uttered the seed-syllable of speech, Bhuvaneśvarī, and the words "speak, speak," one [meditates on] Vāgvādinī.
Svāhā Vāgvādini! I meditate upon the eternal Speech, who has cast off the burden of the multitude of sins through her colors,
and who holds a lute, a book, a rosary, a bangle, and a blossoming lotus.
She bore in her palms rays of reddish light, manifesting a burgeoning grace.

Regarding "Vāk": having uttered the mantra "I meditate upon Vāgīśvarī, the eternal speech," what is it? It is the seed-syllable of speech, the syllable *Aiṃ*; and [the syllable of] Bhuvaneśvarī, the syllable *Hrīṃ*; followed by "speak, speak, O speaker of speech, svāhā."

Of what nature was that speech? It was such that the burden of sins was shattered—that is, removed—by its syllables, meaning by the letters of the mantra. Furthermore, of what nature was that speech? It held a lute, a book, a rosary-bead bracelet, and a lotus with its four palms, that is, the soles of its hands.
She should be understood here as holding, in order from the lower right hand downwards:
a lute with the lower right hand, a book with the lower left hand, a rosary with the upper right hand, and a lotus with the upper left hand; what kind of lotus? One that is blossoming.
The meaning is "fully blossomed. By what kind of palms? Those possessing reddish rays, that is, a crimson luster.
Furthermore, of what nature is the speech? It is one whose grace (*vibhrama*)—meaning its charm—is becoming manifest, that is, appearing clearly. Because it is easy to perform, the mantra...
Just as: Aiṃ Hrīṃ vada vada vāgvādinī svāhā || 19 ||
Now he speaks of the fruit resulting from the recitation and meditation upon the Bhagavatī:
"Therefore, O Mother, by your compassion, cause the sovereignty of the Vidyā to surge forth even more intensely within me."
He whose fame is the sole throne to be served by poets— theft of the moonlight’s fragrance—
and who fills the belly of the vast expanse of worlds, from the fire of time (*kālāgni*) to Śiva.
It is the abode of supreme bliss, made full by the ripening of the waters of wisdom. || 20 ||

"O Mother"—he says: "Therefore, O Mother, for that reason, by means of the recitation and meditation upon you, manifest most intensely (taraṅgyatarām) the sovereignty over the sciences (vidyānām ādhipatyam) within me; by what kind of grace (kṛpā), that is, compassion (anukampā)? Of what nature [is it]?"

The sovereignty of knowledge; the unique lion-throne served by poets, whose fame is like a thief of the fragrance of moonlight—moonlight being *jyotsnā*, its "fragrance" (*saurabha*) being its captivating quality, and the fame that steals it away like a thief;
such is the poetry, which, by this description, is like the beauty of the moonlight.
That which is to be served by her poetry is the single lion-throne; furthermore, what kind of sovereignty over knowledge is it? It is the abode beginning with Kālī and ending with Śivā.
The "limit" (*avasāna*) is the point of cessation for this world; by this, the fivefold activity (*pañcakṛtyatā*) of Śiva is indeed described.

Of such a world, that which is the "prior mass" (*prāgbhāra*)—the prior state consisting of the act of supporting—is the duty of Viṣṇu, meaning protection. The "intellect" (*prajñā*) is that which belongs to Viṣṇu, the former sustainer, and which possesses the quality of filling his own belly (*kukṣiṃbharitā*).
That very water is the moisture; its maturation is the state of transformation; its fullness of bliss is its foundation;
and the locus of that foundation is the commencement of the command of Time (Kāla), which is the Lord (Īśvara)—by the word "and so forth" (ādi), practice and knowledge are also understood.

"Ending in Śiva" refers to the time of attaining the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) and so forth; that itself is the "ending in Śiva. Its "becoming" is its arising; its "forepart" is its prior state;
its "belly-filling" is the water of wisdom—that is, the abundant water of gnosis; and of that... [the remainder follows].
Maturity is transformation; its "thick supreme bliss" (pīnaparānanda) is that which is full of supreme bliss; the foundation of that is its established state, and that is the locus or abode. || 20 ||
16) Now, he describes the seed, the locus, and the fruit of the Bhagavatī by means of a pair of verses:

With lines like those of the moon, the seed-syllable of Speech (Vāgbīja) shines intensely; it is surrounded on all sides by the formidable dot (bindu) in the form of a star, encircled thrice by the Māyā syllable (Hrīṃ),
and this entire [mantra] is situated within the belly of the full moon, its letters white as nectar.
He who, remaining motionless at the tip of his tongue, remembers the stream accumulated through agitation. || 21 ||
By the mere transmission of even a single drop of your compassionate glance, the long-standing dullness within his heart— the foremost of all waking disturbances— attains peace;
therefore, [grant] that which swiftly bestows the realization of the non-duality of the wondrous aesthetic flavor of the three worlds.
An exquisite fragrance arises from the lotus-face through the playful grace of her words.

*Lekheti*— O Mother, that person who [meditates on] the seed-syllable of speech (*vāgbīja*), the syllable *Aiṃ*, which is as if fashioned from the crescents of the moon, and which further flashes intensely above with a dot (*bindu*)— the nasal *anusvāra*— which is both formidable and charming like the form of a star; and which is surrounded on all sides by the triple-layered *māyā*.

It is surrounded on all sides by the nature of illusion, that is, by the seed-syllable of Māyā, in three ways— both forward and backward— and thus this entire whole is situated within the belly of the full moon, in the center of the full moon.

One who, being steady and motionless, meditates upon and contemplates at the tip of the tongue— that is, the edge of the palate— the syllable white as nectar, having a color as pure as ambrosia, and which is further filled with the playful splendor of a flowing stream; for that person, [liberation] is indeed certain.
Why does the long-standing dullness within one's own mind reach peace and destruction?
Simply from the transmission of a single drop of Your compassionate sidelong glance; simply from the mere sight of Your compassionate sidelong glance.
Of what nature is this long-standing dullness? It is the foremost of the transformations of the waking state—those transformations in the form of awakening that occur even while one is awake.
"Vikṛtayaḥ" refers to those who are of improper conduct; among them, he is the "agraṇīḥ," meaning the leader or foremost.

The word "tasmāt" serves as a conclusion. "Āśu" means quickly; "vadana-ambhoje" means in the lotus of the face; "param" means supreme or excellent; "saurabhyaṃ" means fragrance (or, according to another reading, beauty); "abhyudeti" means it rises or comes into manifestation.
What is the use of the wanderings of speech, the playful embellishments of words?

Of what nature is that fragrance which bestows the realization of the non-duality of the wondrous aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of the three worlds— that is, it grants the knowledge of the non-dual nature of that very wonder of the three worlds— or alternatively:
Alternatively, in another reading—*jagattrayādbhutarasādvaitapratītipradaiḥ*—this [phrase] may serve as an adjective for the word *girāṃ vibhramaiḥ*. || 22 ||
17) Now, with two verses, the Blessed Lady describes the parts of the body consisting of the *mātṛkā*:
The first [vowel] is the head; then the next is the face; *i* and *ī* are the two eyes; *u* and *ū* are the two ears; *ṛ* and *ṝ* are the two nostrils; the following two letters are the two cheeks;
*lṛ* and *lṝ* are the teeth; and the diphthongs (*e*, *ai*, *o*, *au*) are, in order, the pair of upper and lower lips.
The root of the tongue is the vowel *u*, the tip is *ū*; the neck is the *visarga* vowel *e*. || 23 ||
The letters beginning with *ka* are on the right arm, and the other group (*ca*, etc. is on the left arm;
*ṭa* and so forth, and *ta* and so forth, are in sequence on the two feet;
*pa* and *pha* are on the two sides of the belly; the letter *va* is on the back, and then the three vowels (*ā*, *i*, *u*) are held in the navel and the heart.
O Ambikā, the seven breaths beginning with Ya, followed by Kṣa and Para, are called Krodha.

Regarding the word "ādya": O Ambikā! Your first letter, *a*, is the crown of your head (*mauli*), and the next, *ā*, is your face. Furthermore, *i* and *ī* are your two eyes; *u* and *ū* are your two ears; and *ṛ* and *ṝ* are the two nostrils (*nāsāvaṃśapuṭa*). "Tadanujau" means those which follow them. [Kh]

The pair of lips is the bindu at its tip, the syllable *aṃ*; the root of the tongue is the other vowel, the visarga *aḥ*, which is your neck.

The class beginning with *ka*—namely, the form *ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa*—is your right arm; as for the word "to the right" (*dakṣiṇataḥ*) used here, because the suffix *-tas* is applicable to all case endings, it is employed in the nominative case. The other class, the *ca*-group—namely, the form *ca, cha, ja, jha, ña*—is the left arm.

In the sequence "the group beginning with *ṭ* [is] yours" and "the group beginning with *t* [is] yours," *ṭa-ṭha-ḍa-ḍha-ṇa* is your right foot, and *ta-tha-da-dha-na* is your left foot. O Mother, *pa-pa* (the letters *pa* and *pha*) are your two sides (*kukṣidvaya*).

The right side of the belly is the letter *pa*; the left side of the belly is the letter *pha*. Now, the three beginning with *ba*—namely *ba*, *bha*, and *ma*—are the three constituting the backbone (*vaṃśa*) located at the back. The backbone consists of the navel, the heart, and the back;

the letter *ba* is the back, the letter *bha* is the navel, and the letter *ma* is the heart. The seven elements (*dhātavaḥ*) beginning with *ya* are those starting with *ya*. Thus, "beginning with *ya*" refers to *ya*.
Your seven constituents (dhātus) are of the nature of *ra*, *la*, *va*, *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and [ha]; they are skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen.
Their locations are the base (*ādhāra*), the genitals, the navel, the heart, the mouth, the space between the eyebrows, and the head.
Furthermore, the seventh is the letter *ha*, which is the wind, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the palate;
O Mother, the letter *kṣa* is your wrath and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). || 24 ||
18) Now, he states the fruit of worshiping the body composed of the letters of the Bhagavatī—[kh: he states the worship]:
O Śivā, he who worships this body of yours composed of letters— which pervades the three worlds—
by means of the letters assigned to its limbs through the contemplation of "I," [perceives you] having become manifest at the close of day in the form of lotuses.
The sciences wait upon him with palms joined, eager for the favor of his glance. || 25 ||
"Thus"—O Śivā! in this manner, that person who worships—that is, takes refuge in—your body composed of phonemes (*varṇamaya*) which pervades the three worlds; by what means?

By means of the phonemes superimposed upon the limbs, that is, the parts of the body, through the contemplation of "I" (*ahaṃbhāvanā*), thinking "I myself am composed of phonemes"—that person [is as described].

The fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyā*), having become personified—that is, having taken on embodied forms—worship him with their palms. Of what nature are these sciences? They are "eager for the grace of his glance," meaning they are anxious, thinking, "He will bestow favor upon us with his look. They rest upon his head, being seated firmly on his crown.

Furthermore, by what kind [of things]? By those whose forms at the close of day resemble lotuses; that is to say, those whose shapes at the time of evening are like the form of lotuses—meaning, they have the shape of buds. || 25 ||
Now, by means of meditation, the Blessed Lady states another result:
those who know, recite constantly, intensely contemplate, or sing—
Their mouths are served by playful utterances with gentle word-placements;

moreover, their fame— flowing like auspicious sandalwood paste and possessing the beauty of the splendor of the white night-lotus of the Kārttika festival— sports throughout the realms of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svar.
"Ya iti"— O Mother, those persons who thus know your form composed of letters (*varṇamaya*),
or worship it, or constantly meditate upon it, or sing it; their face— that is, the mouth of those persons— [is graced] by the play of words, that is, by speech.

By what kind of playful expressions is he worshipped? By the playfulness of speech, by the graceful placement of words, and by the composition of tender phrases. It is not only that, moreover, for those men, [his fame] pervades the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svar—that is, it extends throughout the Bhūrloka and the other realms.
Her fame sports, pervading the Bhuvarloka and Svarloka. Of what nature is this fame?

It is that which creates the auspicious beauty and splendor of the luster of the multitude of white water-lilies (*kairava*) that bloom at night during the month of Kārtika; that is, it produces the beautiful radiance of the fortune of those nocturnal clusters of lilies. Furthermore—
Of what nature is she? She is "exuding glorious sandalwood," meaning she exudes—that is, flows with—glorious sandalwood as if it were nectar.
[Kh: she exudes; G: she exudes and flows with the liquid of glorious sandalwood nectar. || 26 ||
19) Now, by means of another meditation on the body composed of specific syllables, he states another result [of that body].

Furthermore, those who know the tradition of the *Dīpa* recite this [mantra] interspersed with the seed-syllable of Māyā as proclaimed in the *Śrīkūrmacakra*; indeed, the lords of men always serve the feet of such [practitioners], upon which jewel-sprouts rest within the crevices of their crowns.
The beauty of their body-unguents was mingled with the dust of the earth, which was thickened by moonlight.
"O Mother! Furthermore, this body of yours, consisting of letters, is interlaced with the seed-syllable of Māyā—
that is, woven together with the Māyā-bīja— and moreover, it is proclaimed in the Śrī Kūrma-cakra by those people who are constantly conversant with the Dīpāmnāya."
Indeed, those virtuous ones certainly recite [the mantra]; for them, the lords of men—the kings—constantly and eternally attend upon their conduct. Of what nature are these lords of men?
They are such that the dust of the earth, thickened by the moonlight of jewel-sprouts resting upon the eaves of their crowns, mingles with their fragrant unguents.

Those jewels which are rested and settled—their sprouts possess the lovely luster of moonbeams; by means of that, the dust of the earth's surface is made thick, very glossy, and endowed with brilliance. Those whose beauty of bodily unguent is mixed with that [dust] are thus described. This is the "tradition of lamps" (dīpāmnāya).
Having drawn eight squares in the order of emanation, having written pairs of vowels beginning with *a* in each square,
and then having written the letters beginning with *ka* in their collective form, in whichever square—
In whichever place the first letter of the name of the local lord— the deity presiding over the village—
occurs, having placed there the seed-syllable of Māyā (the syllable *hrīṃ*) interwoven with that seed-syllable, [one should perform the rite].
Those who recite the body composed of the Mātṛkā [or Māyā], which is woven together according to the method of *vidarbha*, are called knowers of the Dīpāmnāya; and so it has been said:
One should first draw two by two the vowels, and likewise the consonants beginning with *ka* in the form of groups of letters;
where the letter of the presiding deity of the location resides, the sages call that the "lamp-sign" (*dīpadeśa*).
Now, he describes another result through a different mode of meditation upon the Blessed Lady’s body composed of syllables:
"The seed-syllable of Śrī [is placed] among all the letters and so forth, and again at the end of the wrathful syllables."
And for him who worships the God and this very form of Yours, O Mother, You remain awake before him.

The Goddess of Fortune, as if bound by a beautiful chain formed by rows of bees blinded by their longing for the waves of fragrance from the ichor of oceanic elephants, never departs from him anywhere. 28.

Regarding the phrase "the seed-syllable of Śrī": O Mother! at the beginning of all letters—that is, the first among the phonemes starting with 'a'—is the seed-syllable of Śrī, which takes the form *śrīṃ*. Furthermore, at the end of the letters of wrath [at the end of the letter *kṣa*], there should likewise be the seed-syllable of Śrī. In this manner, whatever man [recites] this of yours...
*Tanuṃ* Śrīṃ Aṃ Śrīṃ Āṃ Śrīṃ Iṃ Śrīṃ Īṃ Śrīṃ, and so on up to *Kṣa*:
[Śrīṃ Aṃ Śrīṃ Āṃ Śrīṃ Iṃ Śrīṃ Īṃ Śrīṃ Uṃ Śrīṃ Ūṃ Śrīṃ Ṛṃ Śrīṃ Ṝṃ Śrīṃ Ḷṃ Śrīṃ Ḹṃ Śrīṃ Eṃ Śrīṃ Aiṃ Śrīṃ Oṃ Śrīṃ Auṃ Śrīṃ Aṃ Śrīṃ].
Aḥ śrīṃ kaṃ śrīṃ khaṃ śrīṃ gaṃ śrīṃ ghaṃ śrīṃ ṅaṃ śrīṃ caṃ śrīṃ chaṃ śrīṃ jaṃ śrīṃ jhaṃ śrīṃ ñaṃ śrīṃ ṭaṃ śrīṃ ṭhaṃ śrīṃ ḍaṃ śrīṃ ḍhaṃ śrīṃ ṇaṃ śrīṃ taṃ śrīṃ thaṃ śrīṃ daṃ śrīṃ dhaṃ śrīṃ naṃ śrīṃ.

For one who worships the body composed of the Mātṛkā, interwoven with the Śrī-bīja: *paṃ śrīṃ, phaṃ śrīṃ, baṃ śrīṃ, bhaṃ śrīṃ, maṃ śrīṃ, yaṃ śrīṃ, raṃ śrīṃ, laṃ śrīṃ, vaṃ śrīṃ, śaṃ śrīṃ, ṣaṃ śrīṃ, saṃ śrīṃ, haṃ śrīṃ, laṃ śrīṃ, kṣaṃ śrīṃ*— for him [the goal is attained].
In front of the man, Lakṣmī, whose abode is the lotus, remains awake and sleepless; she never departs to any other place. Of what nature is Lakṣmī?
She is envisioned as if she were followed by the waves of the fragrance of the ichor from the frontal lobes of elephants.

The "wave of fragrance" is the diffusion of the scent of that ichor (*mada*) which is the secretions of the lordly elephants of Sindhu; the "greed" for it is the intent to seize it; blinded by that greed and agitated, the row of flower-suckers—the swarm of bees—is itself a *bandurā* (a small boat).
She is as if restrained, as if bound, by that heart-captivating chain; [just as anyone else who is bound does not go elsewhere, so it is]. || 28 ||
Now, by means of another meditation, the Blessed Lady speaks again of another fruit:
"He who meditates upon you— who are like a line of coral shoots and sprouts, yet not red— as Māyā, with the three folds of your waist quivering all around him."

For him, those various women—whose lovely sandalwood paste, moonlight, plantains, and pearl necklaces are now objects of reproach, and who are overwhelmed by the dense heat of sighs, delusions, and tears—faint away. (29)

Regarding the word "ya" (she who): O Mother! she who, all around herself—that is, in the vicinity of her own self—perceives you as consisting of the liquid of coral sprouts (*vidrumapallavadravamayī*), meaning having the nature of the spreading of coral shoots [or, alternatively, made from the liquid, i.e., the sap, of coral shoots], and thus entirely red or crimson.

For that person who meditates upon Māyā—who is like a line marked by three throbbing folds, whose form is the syllable *hrīṃ*, and who resides within the shimmering triangle—for the sake of that man, various women endowed with all excellent qualities become infatuated; that is, they fall into a state of delusion. Of what nature are they?
Women whose beauty surpasses sandalwood, the moon, plantains, and strings of pearls (p. 21); [g: + sandalwood and the moon].

They were women by whom even the groves of plantain trees, the plantain forest, and garlands of pearls were disparaged—those [women] who surpassed the sandalwood, the moon, the plantain groves, and the pearl necklaces. Furthermore, what were these women like?
They were dense with the heat of sighing, dizziness, and tears; "dense" (*gahanāḥ*) here refers to being filled by the movement, the release, and the agitation caused by their sighs.
That which is vapor and heat is itself the burning; by that they are dense and agitated. (Alternatively:
the "whirl" is the turning of the sighs; the "tears" are the tears; and the "burning" is the internal fever; by these they are dense and agitated. || 29 ||
Now, by means of another meditation on the Blessed Lady, he speaks of a further result:

"O Mother! He who meditates upon you—who are adorned with the divine scriptures under the name Śrī-Bhagamālinī and who consist of bliss—he indeed possesses the beauty of a woman with beautiful eyebrows."
With their bosoms pressed by arms crossed in the svastika posture, with humble and affectionate words,
and with eyes half-closed in meditation, their pupils dense with horripilation, they meditate. || 30 ||

"O Mother"—this is the form of address; O Mother! that man who [with the name] Śrī Bhagamālinī, [reciting] "Aiṃ Hrīṃ Ānandamayī Bhagamālini Svāhā," [worships] you, who are adorned by the divine scriptures.

The women with curved brows and excellent complexions meditate upon that man who contemplates you—who are adorned and made into a crest-ornament in the divine scriptures (divyāgama), such as the Śaivāgamas and the Rudrayāmala—being composed of bliss and whose very nature is bliss; with what [limbs] do they meditate? With their breasts; of what kind? [They meditate] with their breasts.
By what means? By the pressure of the "arm-svastika" (*bāhusvastika*), that is, by the circle of their staff-like arms arranged in the form of a *svastika*; furthermore, by what?
By the slopes of their breasts marked with sprouts of horripilation (*pulakāṅkura*); and by what else? By endearments (*cāṭu*), that is, by words of affection.
With what kind of flatteries? With those accompanied by wretchedness, such as "I shall become your slave.
Furthermore, with what kind of side-glances from the corners of the eyes (*netrāñcala*)—meaning with sidelong glances (*kaṭākṣa*)? Of what nature are they?
Unobstructed (*nīrandhra*), steady (*niścala*), devoid of the action of movement, and moreover, restrained (*niyamita*).

The meaning is: by those who, through the act of looking at that [object], have made other things their objects of vision—though they are not actually made objects [of the mind]—and who are intent upon looking at that very thing. || 30 ||
Now, furthermore, he describes another fruit by means of another meditation through a pair of verses [these two verses are explained separately in manuscript *kh*]:
"He who meditates upon you, who are like a ship of vermilion for crossing the ocean of passion..."
She sits at ease upon a lotus-throne made of ruby, reclining on a seat of red lotuses;
her body and garments are suffused with the luster of unguents and ornaments, which are composed of rows of radiant gems that rival the splendor of the rising sun.
The women remembered [him]. || 31 ||
Camphor in the form of a white water-lily, a lotus leaf, the skill of the arts, and the tumultuous surge of the "kuhū" cries from flocks of warbling, passionate female cuckoos.
Afflicted by the force of the great epilepsy of passion, which is like the fire of universal destruction,
they tremble, they fall, alas, they cannot utter a word, and they grieve.

As for the word "yaḥ" (who): O Mother! that man who, within the interior of the vermilion boat that crosses the ocean of passion, [sees you] seated upon a lotus-flower made of ruby that is spontaneously blooming by its own will—spontaneously meaning according to its own desire, and "blooming" meaning fully opened.

"Nalinīpuṣpa" means a lotus flower; she who sits upon that very seat is so described. For the man who meditates upon you in such a manner, beautiful women—being full of longing—attain him (this is the meaning). Of what nature are those women?
Clad in the rays of the morning sun... [it is to be observed before them: they suspect camphor;
they do not merely censure camphor alone, but furthermore the bed of night-lotuses, the rows of water-lilies, and even that very lotus leaf—what indeed is their skill in the arts? Of the arts...

This skill is not merely this alone; furthermore, there is the tumultuous roar of the surging waves of the *kuhū* sounds produced by the flock of cooing female cuckoos— that is, the flock of sweet-voiced birds (*kalakaṇṭhī*) making indistinct sounds,
whose clamor arises from the utterance of the *kuhū* cry.
Upon the repeated utterance of the word *kuhū*, women—
agitated by the force of the great epilepsy of Smara, who is like the fire of universal destruction (*pralayānala*)—
tremble; for that very Smara is the Vaiśvānara fire belonging to the time of cosmic dissolution.

By that impulse which is like a great seizure (mahāpasmāra), they become afflicted and tormented; they tremble, cry out "Alas! in distress, and fall completely to the earth. Furthermore, they do not release nor utter any speech or voice.
Furthermore, having regained consciousness, they grieve because he has not been found;

likewise, anyone else who becomes afflicted by the force of amnesia trembles, falls down, and cannot utter a word, and then, having regained consciousness, grieves, thinking, "What sin have I committed? by which [this occurred].
"A disease like epilepsy has arisen in me. What were those women like?
Their limbs were joined with the brilliance of rows of ornaments upon their various members—jewels whose luster rivaled the rising young sun;
they thus emulated the young, red sun as it first began its ascent.
The "rivalries" (*sapatnāni*) are those of the sun that hates (*dviṣanti*) and rivals (*sapanti*); the ornaments for every limb (*pratyaṅgabhūṣāḥ*) fashioned and constructed from those jewels;
and the splendors (*rucayaḥ*), which are rows of radiance (*kāntipaṅktayaḥ*), belonging to those [ornaments].

Those whose body-unguents and garments were blended and mixed with those [rays], such [are they]. [Regarding the word *tasya*: it is either a genitive used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhī*), or it is an accusative.]
If it ends in the nominative case, it is an epithet of the Goddess. || 32 ||
23) Now, he describes the propitiation of the mantra of Mṛtyuñjaya belonging to the Bhagavatī: [G: he describes the propitiation by means of the mantra].
O Hrīṃkāri, you who are the essence of the Blessed One Caitanyacandra named Śrīmṛtyuñjaya, O Saṃjīvinī, dispel the primordial darkness!

I worship you, the Sovereign of the Svāhā-clasping arms, with the impetuosity of attaining my own innate awakening; make me, whose heart-knot is expanding through the vital breath, abide as the living soul within you. 33.
O Śrīti! O you who are the moonlight of the consciousness of the Blessed Lord Śambhu, whose name is Mṛtyuñjaya—for she is of the same nature as that moonlight because of its illuminating quality!

O Hrīṃkārī! O Reviver of the Swan (Haṃsa)! O Haṃsasañjīvinī! [g: O you whose name is Mṛtyuñjaya; such is the Blessed Lord Śambhu’s consciousness itself, which is like moonlight because of its illuminating nature; O Hrīṃkārī! O Haṃsasañjīvinī! O Haṃsa... [g: O...]

O Haṃsa-saṃjīvanī! [The address to her who revives the *haṃsa*—the *brahman* devoid of qualities—and renders it known as the individual soul (*jīva*): Out of the impetuosity of attaining my own awakening—that is, through the joy of acquiring self-knowledge—I worship you, the sovereign of the gods who consume the sacrificial oblation (*svāhā*).

Regarding the basis: for this reason, since you are of the nature of the moon (*candrātmikā*) and possess the syllable *hrīṃ* as your first [element], you who are thus constituted, O *Hrīṃkārī*, dispel my primordial darknesses— my former ignorances and so forth (in the reading *prathamātamāṃsi*, there is an elision of the *ś*).
"Rend it! In the phrase *prathamātamāṣi*, there is the elision of the *ṅi* case-ending according to the rule *chandasi ṅiśyor vā lopaḥ*.
Alternatively, [Kh: there is no fault whatsoever here, as *prathame* means 'in the first' or 'at the beginning']. Furthermore, the word *ca* (and) must be supplied here;
and moreover, my life—the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) situated within the knot of the heart that is expanding."
Make [the mantra] abide in— that is, take refuge in— that heart-knot which is yawning open and blossomed;

(in the context of the extraction of the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra, however, it refers to the syllable *hrīṃ*, which consists of the word "Bhagavat" in the name "Śrīmṛtyuñjaya," followed by the words "Caitanya" and "Candra").
Where the word *svāhā* follows the syllable *śrīṃ* after the first letter, she whose arm is for the purpose of accepting the substances offered by devotees and for granting their desires;
as is the mantra of Mṛtyuñjaya: *oṃ*. [Note: In manuscript *kh*, the *praṇava* (syllable *oṃ*) does not appear in this mantra.]
Śrīṃ hrīṃ, O Blessed One, O Conqueror of Death, O Moon of Consciousness, O Reviver of the Haṃsa, svāhā! || 33 ||
Now he describes the meditation named Mṛtyuñjaya [Kh, G: and states the fruit of Mṛtyuñjaya for the Supreme Sovereign]:
"In this way, day after day, you who are the Mistress of Nectar, the beloved of the full moon..."
But those who directly worship Him, whose form is perpetually manifest within their own hearts,
place their foot upon the head of Death, even as he swallows the entire expanse of the three worlds.
Having given [these], they sport with various pleasures in the great ocean of enjoyments without end. || 34 ||

Thus it is said: "O Mother! those men, having placed their left foot upon the head or crown of Death (Kṛtānta), sport and revel in the ocean of enjoyment as long as they wish, with various pleasures such as wealth, wife, sons, horses, elephants, and so forth. Of what sort is Death?"

Of you, whose enjoyment consists of the entirety of the three worlds swallowed as a single morsel— [that is,] of him for whom there is an all-encompassing experience (*bhoga*) of that triple world which has been swallowed and consumed—
who indeed are those men who possess such characteristics as previously described?

They worship you daily and incessantly, directly as Amṛteśvarī, the bestower of liberation, who possesses the characteristics previously described; how so? You, whose form shines perpetually within the hearts of the lover of the night of the full moon—that is, the lover of the night (*niśākāmuka*) of *rākā*, the full moon.
She whose body (vapuḥ) shines constantly within—that is, in the midst (antaḥ)—of the moon;
she is such, and [he refers to] her. || 34 ||
Now, the Supreme Goddess describes the meditation on the *mṛtyuñjaya-mantra*:
Having flooded all directions with the mass of nectar-rays of waking consciousness, ...

May that eternal Bhuvaneśvarī, whose every art is free from blemish, who traverses the six chakras, who is uniquely skilled in shattering the darkness of wretchedness, and who extends the supreme speech— sport in my mind like a swan. (35)
"Awakened"—may that eternal Bhuvaneśvarī, whose nature is consciousness and whose form is the syllable *hrīṃ*, sport and play within my mind, within my heart. Like what? Like a female swan (*haṃsī*);
just as a female swan sports in a lotus lake (*mānasa-saras*), so may she do. Who is she? She who is Bhuvaneśvarī.

A certain undefiled digit, the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*), traverses the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*) and, having pierced the six wheels, becomes instantly arisen; having done what? Having flooded—that is, pervaded—all directions with what?
With the mass of rays consisting of the nectar of supreme awakening (*tāgrabodha-sudhā*). That very knowledge (*jñāna*) which is the nature of the supreme awakening while awake—[with that].
By means of those masses of rays—that is, the collections of her beams—which are like nectar; what kind of digit?

One that is uniquely skilled in tearing asunder the darkness of wretchedness; "wretchedness" here is ignorance, which is itself the darkness, a dense gloom, and she is uniquely expert in its tearing asunder—that is, in its total dispelling. Furthermore...
Of what nature is this supreme art? It is that which extends the highest speech—that is, it extends and expands the voice that proclaims the supreme.
Now, [the author] speaks of the Supreme Goddess as being none other than these:
You alone are the mother and father; You alone are friends; You are brothers; You are companions; You are knowledge; You are noble fame and conduct; You are most wonderful fortune.
Furthermore, O Śrī Viśveśvarī, having understood that all my desires are fulfilled, be gracious; O Mother, you are my refuge, for there is no other for me. (36)
O Mother! O you who are tender with compassion! O Sovereign of the Universe! Be gracious; grant me your full favor, for I have no other refuge whatsoever besides you.

Having understood what? It is as follows: "O Mother, you alone are my mother and father—my *jananī* and *janaka*; the word 'alone' (*eva*) here serves to emphasize this distinction. Furthermore, you alone are my friends (*suhṛdaḥ*), you alone are my brothers and kinsmen (*bhrātaraḥ*, *bāndhavāḥ*), you alone are my companion (*sakhā*), and you alone are the fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyāḥ*). Therefore, that noble conduct and fame [is yours]."
You alone are the one who causes the great fame to spread; you alone are that most wonderful and abundant fortune.
