Furthermore, what more need be said? You alone are everything desired and all that is wished for. || 36 ||
Now he states the name of the Guru, which brings about supreme accomplishment: "In this fourth age, a certain Śrīsiddhinātha, an ocean of compassion, appeared."
By the name Śrīśambhu, that sovereign of all the Āgamas made his mind gracious toward me. (37)

Regarding the name "Śrī Siddhinātha": in the village called Karuṇāvaruṇālaya—a residence of compassion, endowed with mercy, and situated near the banks of the Narmadā—there appeared in the fourth age, the Kali Yuga, a certain person known as Śrī Siddhinātha. What was his nature? Regarding that Śrī Siddhinātha:
By name Śrīśambhu, he made my heart and mind clear—that is, he showed affection toward me. Furthermore, what was Śrīśambhu like?
He was the sovereign of the entire circle of scriptures (*sakalāgamacakravartin*), meaning he who moves within the circle of all the scriptures (*sakaleṣv āgameṣu cakravartī*).

Regarding the phrase "independent of all systems" (*sarvatantrasvatantra*): what kind of being is this Śrīsiddhinātha? The meaning is that he is the abode of compassion, an ocean of mercy. Thus, this serves as an epithet for the word *asmin* ("in this"), which refers to the Siddha. || 37 ||
Now, manifesting an abundance of compassion, he says:
"By his command, those who have perfected the lineage and attained vidyā— "

Therefore, O Goddess of the World, O Embodiment of the Vedas, be pleased at once by these playful expressions of speech consisting of words of praise that serve as the basis for distinction; manifest Your presence within my mouth. (38)

Regarding the word "tasya" (of him): O Bhuvaneśvarī! O Vedagarbhā! since that venerable Śambhu has made my mind—directed toward me as his object—well-pleased, for this very reason, you should immediately, at that very moment, be gracious; be intent upon showing favor. Therefore, following that grace, for me...
Be present—make your appearance—in his mouth with the playful charms of words; with what kind of charms?
With words of praise, that is, expressions suited for hymns of adoration. Furthermore, with what kind of charms?
With those which, by his command, have become the locus for the various branches of perfected knowledge (vidyā) whose lineages have reached maturity.

By the command of Śrīśambhu, the lineage—the tradition and succession of gurus—has reached its full development; [the phrase "tathā"] means by those various points of division and locations of differentiation belonging to the perfected sciences (siddhavidyā) within that lineage. || 38 ||
Now he expresses his prayer to the Blessed Lady:
"O Mother, for those for whom you are the supreme family deity,
let my words not be mingled with their speech."
I entreat you that there may never be, even for a moment, dwelling upon an object once it has been familiarized by them; rather, let there be constant [abiding]. 39.

Regarding the phrase "yeṣām": O Sovereign of All! I constantly and incessantly entreat you thus: O Mother! May my words not be mingled with the speech of those men for whom you are not the supreme family deity; nor, moreover, with them.
Even in a region or country familiar to men— where one has attained acquaintance, where one has gained familiarity,
and even in a land inhabited by one's father, grandfather, great-grandfather, and so forth— let there never be, even for a single moment, a dwelling there; let it not be.
Now, supplicating the Guru, he says:
"O Śrī Śambhunātha! O Compassionate One! O Siddhinātha! O Śrī Siddhinātha! O Compassionate One! O Śambhunātha!"
Even though I am stained by every transgression, make your mind well-disposed toward me; take refuge in me, for there is no other. 40.
"O Śrīśambhunātha!"—O Śrīśambhunātha! O Karuṇākara Siddhinātha!
O Śrīsiddhinātha, Karuṇākara Śambhunātha! Even toward me, who am stained by every offense and defiled by all transgressions, please make your mind gracious and compassionate.
For this reason, I have no other refuge whatsoever. || 40 ||
27) Now [the author] speaks of the compassion of the Supreme Goddess:
"In this manner, with eyes brimming with tears at every moment..."
Before Pṛthvīdhara, she clearly manifested;
having granted him the boon, the Blessed Lady entered his heart, and she herself descended into his mouth through ever-new scriptures. (41)

"Thus"— that is, in this manner, from the recollection of the Guru and so forth, at every moment, for Pṛthvīdhara, whose eyes were overflowing with tears, with tears streaming profusely from his eyes.

The Blessed Lady Bhuvaneśvarī appeared clearly and manifestly right before one's eyes; having become manifest, she entered the heart after bestowing a boon. Furthermore, the Blessed Lady herself, by means of ever-new scriptures composed of prose, verse, and so forth—
Having entered the mouth, it has attained expansion. || 41 ||
Now, he speaks of the grace bestowed regarding the subject of praise:
"Having thus observed this incomparable perfection of speech, the Lord Śrī Śambhu [granted] even that great *pratiṣṭhā* (establishment) for him."
He remained for a very long time in his own station, which was uniquely beautiful as the lion-throne of learning, venerated by the scriptures of the three worlds. || 42 ||

Regarding the word "vāk": O Lord Śrīśambhu, having beheld my speech, grant me incomparable and abundant perfection of speech (*vāksiddhi*) in this world, so that it may endure for a long time in this very place through the mere recitation of this hymn.

He established a most exalted and great foundation that bestows all perfections (*siddhi*). In what kind of state? In his own state, which was uniquely beautiful because of its throne of knowledge (*vidyā-siṃhāsana*) that is worthy of praise and worship by the scriptures (*āgama-śāstra*) of the three worlds—that is, by whatever scriptural treatises exist within the three worlds.
"It is beautiful; so be it," he said regarding that. || 42 ||

Now he describes the procedure for the occasion of mantra recitation: sleeping on the ground, restraint of speech, abstention from women, morning oblations of *jāti* wood twigs, and the purification of the teeth and tongue.
On the leaf-plate, there is sweet food; with the flowers of the *brahmavṛkṣa*, one performs worship and fire-offerings; and there are radiant flowers, garments, and unguents. (43)

Regarding the phrase "on the ground": sleeping on the ground is *bhūmiśayana*; restraint of speech is *vāksaṃyama*, which is turning away from passionate women, that is, abstaining from women; likewise, at dawn—that is, in the morning—there is the purification of the teeth and the tongue using twigs of the *jātī* tree as tooth-sticks (*viṭapa-samidh*). This refers to the cleaning of the teeth and the tongue.
Purification means making stainless; the *patrāvalī* is well known.

In it, one should perform worship and fire-offerings (*pūjā-homa*) with sweet food, such as rice-milk (*udana*, etc.), and with the flowers of the *brahmavṛkṣa*—that is, the flowers of the *palāśa*. Likewise:

Flowers, garments, and ointments that are radiant—[kh, g: likewise, flowers and garments that are radiant; "flowers" refers to blossoms such as the *śatapatra* and others; "garments" refers to white clothes; likewise, "ointments" consist of those derived from sandalwood and other substances—all these are radiant. || 43 ||

Now he states what occurs from the recollection of the Guru— or, according to some versions, from the recitation of the hymn— by one established in the vow for three months without interruption at dawn: "In this manner, he who remains steadfast in the vow for three full months at dawn..."
At midday or at the time of sunset, one should recite it with a single-pointed mind;
through its abundant manifestations, which are a source of wonder for the entire world.
All sciences [appeared] instantaneously in his mouth through the grace of Śambhunātha. 44.

"In this manner"— that is, in this way, the man who, remaining established in his vow for three months, without fail and continuously, at dawn in the morning time, or at midday, or at the time of sunset in the evening, remains single-minded;

Having become single-minded, one should recite, read, and contemplate the praise of the glorious Guru; for that person, at that very moment, all sciences will suddenly flash forth from the mouth with joy in the form of prose, verse, and so forth.

Why? Through the grace of Śambhunātha, by means of abundant ecstasies that are immediately manifest in form and which cause wonder throughout all the worlds— what is not obtained within the three worlds through the remembrance of the Guru?
Rather, the meaning is that the entirety [of the result] is indeed obtained. || 44 ||

Now, he describes the greatness of the hymn according to its true power: "Even one who is devoid of vows and has not obtained the mantras, if purified by faith, should recite [or: chant] it when it has dawned."
For him as well, within a year, there arise sciences that are faultless, immediately effective, and pleasing as poetic compositions. || 45 ||
Regarding the phrase "by means of the vow" (vratena): that person who, although devoid of a vow and having not yet acquired the mantras— that is, one who has not obtained the mantras—
becomes purified by faith, having a mind cleansed through faith, [practices] day after day.

If one recites this continuously, then for that person, after a year—that is, a full year—the sciences become manifest and radiant; how so? They are "heart-pleasing through faultless and immediate poetic power," meaning they are delightful through flawless, immediate poetic composition (*kavitva*), that is, through poetry arising at that very moment.
Captivating. || 45 ||
Now he speaks of the inconceivable majesty of this hymn:
"The power of this hymn is some inconceivable thing that brings about conviction;
by the command of Śrī Śambhu, all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis) are established within it. (46)
"Kopi" means that this hymn possesses an inconceivable power that brings about conviction and generates joy;
for this reason, by the command of the illustrious Śambhu,
all the supernatural powers (siddhis), beginning with *aṇimā*, are established— that is, enshrined— within this hymn, and for that very reason...
The meaning is: "The Hymn to the One of Inconceivable Majesty. || 46 ||
The extensive and pure commentary on the work of Pṛthvīdhara, titled *Sadyuktidīpikā*, has been composed by the poet Padmanābha.
The Lamp of Right Reasoning.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Bhuvaneśvarīstotra*, composed by the poet Śrī Padmanābha. [Kh: the exposition; G: the explanation.]
Written by the Brāhmaṇa Jerāma.
Colophon of the manuscript:
May there be auspiciousness! On the ninth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa in the year 1950, on a Friday, this was the handwriting of Gaṅgāsahāya Śarmā.
May this book bring auspiciousness to Āyodhyaka Sarayūprasāda Dvivedin, during the reign of the illustrious Śrī Savāyī Śrī Mādhavasiṃha in Jayapura.
Colophon of the manuscript: Written by Kedāranātha in the Vikrama Saṃvat 1993; completed today, on the first day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, in Dehlī.

O Mother! This hymn—whether deficient in its measures, its *bindus*, its pairs of syllables, its feet, or its words; whether recited with devotion or without devotion, according to sequence or otherwise, by the force of my own nature; whether manifest or unmanifest; whether read through delusion or ignorance, or perhaps not read at all—I now offer it.
May all that be complete with its constituent parts, O Goddess, bestower of boons upon the three worlds! O Vidyā, be gracious!
Thus ends the *Śrībhuvaneśvarīstotra* composed by the venerable Pṛthvīdhara Ācārya, also known as the *Śrīsiddhasārasvata*, as transcribed by Jayajaya Harikavi Mallabhaṭṭa.
May there be supreme auspiciousness.
Śrī.
Now begins the five-limbed ritual manual (pañcāṅga) of Bhuvaneśvarī; therein, first, the chapter (paṭala).
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Now I shall describe Bhuvaneśvarī, the sustainer of the world;
even Brahmā and the other gods, having known her, attained supreme prosperity (or exalted glory).
The Lord of Nakula is mounted upon fire, possessing a left eye and a half-moon;
this is declared to be his seed-syllable by those desiring complete accomplishment. (2)
The seer is Śakti; the meter is declared to be Gāyatrī;
the deity is Bhuvaneśvarī, who is served by the hosts of gods. (3)
One should perform the ritual assignment of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) by means of the seed-syllables joined with the six long vowels,
according to the path taught by Sarasvatī [by way of the sequence of withdrawal and emanation]. Having assigned the *mātṛkā* to one's body,
one should then perform the assignment of the mantra (*mantranyāsa*) for the sake of attaining the state of the deity.
One should place Hṛllekhā on the head and Gaganā in the lotus of the heart.
One should visualize the red Karālikā at the secret place and Mahocchuṣmā on the two feet;
and [the others] upon the faces in the upward, eastern, southern, northern, and western directions.

The short seed-syllables beginning with *madhya* [i.e., *sadya*], such as the letter *o* (the *sadyojāta* mantra) and the others—the five short vowels *o*, *e*, *u*, *i*, *a*—and the powers (*śaktis*) beginning with *Hṛllekhā* should be installed, radiant with their respective elements.
One should install Brahmā on the forehead, conjoined with the Gāyatrī. || 7 ||
One should place Viṣṇu together with Sāvitrī on the right cheek,
and likewise Maheśvara together with Vāgīśvarī on the left cheek.

Having assigned Gaṇapati with Śrī, and likewise Gaṇapati with Puṣṭi; then, having assigned Dhanapati with Śrī at the tip of the left ear, one should again assign Smara with Rati in the mouth, and likewise Gaṇapati with Puṣṭi [Siṃ Siṃ].
One should place Siddhi above the left ear, and Nidhi between the ear and the cheek. || 9 ||
The root mantra should be placed on the face; then one should place these [syllables] upon the body:
at the base of the throat, on the pair of breasts, on the left shoulder, and in the lotus of the heart. (10)
The instructor [should place the hand] on the left shoulder, on both sides, at the region of the navel,
on the forehead, shoulder, side, and abdomen, on the side and the back of the shoulder, and on the heart.

One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the Brahmāṇīs and the others upon the body according to the prescribed rite and their stated characteristics; then, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa) over the body with the root mantra and meditate upon the Goddess.

I worship Bhuvaneśī, who possesses the splendor of the rising sun, who wears the moon as a crown, whose breasts are lofty, who is endowed with three eyes, whose face is smiling, and whose hands display the gestures of granting boons (*vara*), the goad (*aṅkuśa*), the noose (*pāśa*), and the protection (*abhaya*).
(Regarding the placement of the *vara* and other gestures, it is as stated in the *Padārthādarśa*: "The boon is in the lower left hand...")
In the upper right [hand] is a goad, in the upper left a noose, and in both lower [hands] a bell—so say those who know the tradition. || 13 ||
The knower of mantras should recite the mantra thirty-two lakhs of times according to the prescribed measure;
he should perform oblations with eight substances mixed with the three sweets (ghṛta, madhu,
and śarkarā) in a quantity equal to one-tenth of the recitation.
The eight substances: "The wise know the eight substances to be fuel-sticks of Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Nyagrodha, along with white mustard seeds, milk-rice, and clarified butter. (14)
At that time, the best of practitioners, having meditated upon Pārvatī there, should offer the arghya water to the Lord of Day (the Sun) and draw a lotus-shaped yantra.
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus on the outside and a sixteen-petaled lotus;
in the center of the pericarp, one should draw a most beautiful hexagon.
The Śrīcakra consists of a central point (bindu) and a triangle joined with six-angled figures, adorned with a circle and embellished by eight petals;
it is marked by three circles representing the digits of the moon and the square of the earth, and is endowed with nine powers.
Jayā, Vijayā, then Ajitā, Aparājitā,
Nityā, Vilāsinī, Dogdhrī, Aghorā, and Maṅgalā— these are the nine.
Having offered the seat beginning with the seed-syllable (bīja), one should fashion the form by means of that very [syllable];
therein, having invoked the Goddess, one should worship her along with the enclosures (āvaraṇas) in due order.
In the center, the east, the south, the north, and the west, respectively— [or in the center, the east, the south,
the north, and the west, respectively]—
Hṛllekhā and the others, possessing radiance equal to the five elements, should be worshipped. (20)

Holding a boon-granting gesture, a noose, a goad, and the gesture of fearlessness, and adorned with infinite ornaments, one should worship the deities of the limbs in the locations previously mentioned. (21)
Within the six corners, the practitioner of mantra should thereafter worship the deities of the couples:
in the northeast corner [he should worship her] who holds a shining staff, a water-pot, a rosary, and displays the gesture of fearlessness. (22)
The practitioner of mantras should worship Gāyatrī and likewise Brahmā;
[he should also worship her] in the southwestern corner, holding a discus, a conch, a mace, and a lotus.
One should worship Sāvitrī, dressed in yellow garments, and likewise Viṣṇu in the northwestern corner, holding an axe, a rosary, and displaying the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons.
One should worship Sarasvatī in the west, and Rudra—possessing such characteristics—in the southeast;
one should worship the jewel-pitcher and the jewel-casket in the southeast corner.
[One should meditate on] the pot-bellied Lord of Wealth, who holds a yellow [garment] with both hands;
[the practitioner] embraces him with the right hand, while with the left hand he holds a lotus. (26)
One should worship Mahālakṣmī, who is mounted upon the shoulder of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
In the western quarter, one should worship Madana, who holds an arrow, a noose, a goad, and a bow.

One should worship her who is adorned with jewel ornaments, holding a deep red [or hibiscus-red] lotus, embracing her husband with her right hand while holding a blue lotus with her left; one should properly worship Rati, who stands upon the lap of her lover. (28)
In the northeast (īśāna), one should properly worship Vighnarāja together with his beloved.
The beloved one holds a spear and a noose; his beautiful limbs touch the fingers of the beloved woman.
He carries a skull-cup filled with honey, is the king of colors, and is naked.
He holds a splendid lotus from which radiant gems drip into shimmering goblets; she possesses a form like vermilion, with the unrestrained, playful intoxication of joy.
One should worship the goddess Puṣṭi, who is red in color, naked, embraced by her beloved, and holding a red lotus in one hand while touching the banner of that [deity] with the other. 32.
The two treasures (Nidhis) should be worshipped in the pericarp; then, on both sides of the hexagon, the limbs (Aṅgas);
these [limbs] in the filaments; and afterwards, one should worship them on the petals.
First Anaṅgakusumā, then Anaṅgakusumāruṇā (or Anaṅgakusumāturā);
likewise Anaṅgamadanā, and then Anaṅgamadanāturā. || 34 ||
Bhuvanapālā and Gaganavegā, and after them Śaśirekhā and Gaganarekhā— these are the eight powers (aṣṭaśaktayaḥ). (35)
Holding a noose, a goad, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, they possess ruddy complexions.
Then, upon the sixteen petals, there are Karālī, Vikarālī, and Umā.
Sarasvatī, Śrī, Durgā, Uṣā, Lakṣmī, Śruti, Smṛti, Dhṛti, Śraddhā, Medhā, Mati, Kānti, and Āryā are the sixteen Śaktis. (37)
The Mothers, dark-complexioned and bearing swords and shields, are to be worshipped;
outside the lotus, the attendant Śaktis are to be honored. (38)
She may be Prathamāṅgarūpā, as well as Anaṅgamadanā;
she is Madanāturā, Bhuvanavegā, and Bhuvanapālikā. || 39 ||
There may be a girdle that is the very embodiment of the god of love’s passion for women, and likewise a girdle that is the very embodiment of the coolness of all things that arouse desire;
there may also be a drinking cup, a palm-leaf fan, betel, and a brilliant parasol. (40)
One should worship the three lines of gurus, who hold chowries, silken garments, and flowers in their lotus-like hands, and who are adorned with all ornaments.

One should worship outside the [mandala], in due order, the divine lineages (divyaugha), the perfected lineages (siddhaugha), and the human lineages (mānavaugha), as well as the world-protectors (lokapāla) resplendent with all their ornaments.
Indra, Agni, Yama, Nairṛti, Varuṇa, the Maruts, Kubera, and Īśa are the lords of the directions starting from the east, in order. (43)
An elephant, a ram, a buffalo, a ghost (preta), a crocodile,
a deer, a man, and a bull— these are to be worshipped in order, starting from the east.
The vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, the noose, as well as the goad, the mace, and the trident—these are remembered as the weapons starting from the east. || 45 ||
Brahmā and Viṣṇu are likewise to be worshipped in the upward and downward directions respectively;
[they are seated upon] the swan and the eagle, and the lotus and the disc, through the conjunctions of the directions beginning with the east.
He is worshipped by all the gods, how much more so by the best of men;
having offered oblations of the finest *aśvattha* wood-samids mixed with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), the practitioner of mantras [attains success]. (47)

One should quickly bring Brahmins under control by means of a lotus-homa; one's kings by means of *palāśa* flowers; their wives by means of those same flowers; and ministers by means of *kusuma* (or *kumuda*) flowers. (48)
He who daily sprinkles himself with water consecrated twenty-five times will possess all good fortune. (49)
A person who drinks water consecrated twenty-five times in the morning will necessarily attain great wisdom and become a leader among poets. (50)
Having taken well-prepared saffron mixed with camphor and agallochum, one should apply a tilaka; this is the unsurpassed means for bringing a kingdom under control. (51)
Having fashioned a doll out of rice-flour and mixed with sweet substances,
and having consecrated it by reciting the mantra, one should consume it on a Sunday.

It brings a king, a woman, or even a man under one's control. Standing in water up to the neck and gazing at the sun reflected in the water, one should recite the mantra three thousand times; he shall obtain his desired maiden.
The practitioner of mantra should eat consecrated food for the sake of attaining prosperity.
Having written the non-deceptive [amāyā] mantra, which is easily accomplished, with ashes upon a wooden board or similar surface,
one should display that yantra at that very time; thus, a pregnant woman will give birth easily.

The ritual action to be accomplished is situated within the *śakti*; it is surrounded by fires within the world (*bhuvana*) or abode (*bhavana*), and externally it is joined with the *śaktis* located at the corners— meaning it is joined with the letter *ī* situated at the corners.
"With the bindu" is the traditional teaching (*sampradāya*); its meaning is as follows:

having written the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Bhuvaneśvarī, one should write the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*) in place of its *repha*, the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) in place of its *īkāra*, and the ritual action (*karman*) between those two; then, one should encircle it with the seed-syllables of Bhuvaneśvarī.

Having written the letter *ī* together with its *bindu* within the three corners of the triangle, and having written the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśvarī at each of the tips of the triangle's corners— one in each corner— one should encircle each of those three seed-syllables clockwise with the letter *r*, and join the tips of the *ī*s of one to those of the other. Then:

Having written the four syllables "hari-hara" on the two sides of the three corners, and having drawn three outer circles, one should encircle the two paths situated within them; in the first path, starting from its own front and proceeding clockwise, one should repeatedly write the syllables "ha-ri ī ha-ra ī," and then in the second path—

Having encircled [the central deity] clockwise starting from its own top with the letters of the Mātṛkā, beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣ*, each accompanied by a nasal bindu, one should construct a square on the outermost perimeter; this yantra bestows the aforementioned fruits. And so it is said:
In this case as well, for the sake of prosperity, the practitioner himself, being composed, should worship the Goddess according to the rules and likewise worship Hṛllekhā and the others as before.
Thereafter, one should worship the limbs and then fully worship Gāyatrī and the others:
Gāyatrī at the seed-syllable at the eastern tip, Sāvitrī on the southern edge,
Sarasvatī situated in the northwest (māruta), and likewise Brahmā in the southeast (vahni).
One should worship Viṣṇu and Īśa in the western [quarter], and then Īśa outside of that;
then the Brahmāṇīs and other guardians of the world (lokapālas), and outside of those, the thunderbolt and other [emblems].
In this way, the most excellent practitioner should worship the Goddess with these syllables tripled.
With the syllables *hari*, *hara*, and *iva* placed upon the cheeks,
and subsequently joined again with those same letters, the desired syllable is encircled, bestowing sweet objects of desire.
The *Siṃsiṃ* yantra, situated within a city-diagram (*bhūpura*) and tripled, bestows good fortune and prosperity. (56)

Having written the name of the person to be accomplished situated within the seed-syllable, surrounded by the syllables *śara* (h), *māyā* (hrīṃ), *ramā* (śrīṃ), and *manmatha* (klīṃ), enclosed within two fire-purifiers (*vahni-pura*), and having inscribed the three seeds of Āṣāḍha within the six compartments (*rasapuṭa*).

May that [Self], whose essence is the Self, who is worshipped by Hari and Hara, whose cheeks are adorned with the six seed-syllables externally, and who is surrounded on both sides by the letters of the joints— may He protect you. 57.
One should draw this divine yantra, which possesses sixfold qualities and bestows all perfections upon those who wear it, with its corners radiant with the Cintāmaṇi and Nṛsiṃha;
it is marked externally by sixteen tridents and is exceedingly beautiful.
This yantra, multiplied sixfold, is supreme and brings about all accomplishments.
In this [mandala], the practitioner of mantra should worship the Goddess with whatever is most auspicious for her;
there should be a twelve-petaled lotus endowed with twenty-six filaments.
One should make it beautiful on the outside by arranging the [planetary] signs and so forth;
having worshipped the pedestal endowed with the nine powers, one should invoke the deity.
One should worship with sandalwood and other offerings as before;
and as previously stated, one should perform the six-limbed worship and sacrifice to the couples.
One should worship the twelve external Śaktis in sequence, beginning with Raktā:
Raktā, Anaṅgakusumā, Nityā, and Kusumāturā. || 5 ||
Likewise, Anaṅgamadanā and Madanāturā should be [placed];
Gaurī and Gaganā likewise; the word "gagana" ends with the letter *repha* (ṛ). || 6 ||
The mantra-practitioner who worships Bhuvaneśvarī according to this rite shall become an abode of fortune and be honored by the gods.
"At the end of the body, he attains union with Śiva; this is most certain.
Such is the specific detail in the *Siṃhasiddhāntasindhu*. [The meaning of this is as follows:
there, having drawn a circle by means of a rotation according to one's desired measure, and having struck a Brahma-thread (a north-south axis) therein from east to west...]

Holding the junction of the two tips of that [line], one should form two fish-marks, one in the south and one in the north, using a cord of half the circumference of the circle; when this is done, a set of four fish-marks is produced.
Then, regarding the two eastern fish-marks, [one should draw] from south to north...

Having struck two horizontal lines and placed [the cord] at the eastern tip of the Brahma-line, one should strike two horizontal lines at the two western "fish" (matsya) marks; then, having placed it again at the western tip of the Brahma-line, one should strike two lines within the bellies of the eastern-direction "fish" marks. Thus.
When [the circle] is made, two fire-mandalas arise; then one should erase the circle and the eastward thread.

Having thus formed a hexagon, one should write the seed-syllable of Śakti in its center, write the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) in the portion of its letter *ra*, and write the name of the practitioner (sādhaka) in the portion of its vowel *i*.
One should write the ritual action (*karma*) within the space between the letters *re* and *pha* in the portion belonging to the practitioner; having thus inscribed what is intended,
one should write the seed-syllable of Śakti five times in a circular fashion above the central seed-syllable,
then outside of that, the seed-syllable of Śrī five times, and again outside of that, the seed-syllable of Kāma five times.

In the three upper corners of the hexagon, in the order north, center, and south, one should write the seed-syllables of Śakti, Śrī, and Kāma— one seed-syllable per triangle— each joined with the name of the practitioner. Then, in the three lower triangles, those same seed-syllables, joined with the *visarga* and the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*), should be written in the order south, center, and north.
Having drawn [the diagram], one should write the fourth vowel *ī* together with the bindu (*īṃ*) within the interiors of all six triangles; then,

having written "Hari-Hara" twelve times on both sides of each angle of the hexagon, and having written a single *śakti*-seed-syllable at each of the six tips of the triangles, one should bind them as before, skipping one interval between each.

And it has been stated by the venerable teacher: "Those [lines], separated by single intervals, should be joined to one another. Then, having drawn three circles outside that and produced two paths (vīthī), one should write the letters of the Mātṛkā, from 'A' to 'Kṣa', along with their bindus, in the inner path starting from its own tip and proceeding clockwise.

On the outer path, one should draw those very same letters in the order from *kṣa* to *a*, proceeding clockwise; and it has been stated by the venerable teachers: "On the outside, between the lines, the auspicious letters should be arranged in their proper sequence."
"Furthermore, they may be written in reverse order due to the skill of the scribe.

Thus, having constructed an eight-petaled lotus outside of that, one should write the Nṛsiṃha-bīja to be described later in the four [petals] situated in the cardinal directions, following the sequence of the directions; and in the four corners situated in the intermediate directions, one should write the Cintāmaṇi-bīja to be described later.
Having drawn sixteen lines at the ends of the eight lines situated within the eight corners, one should fashion sixteen tridents;
as stated by the venerable Teacher: "Outside, it is beautiful, marked with sixteen tridents, and possessing distinct colors."
This yantra, multiplied by six, becomes the bestower of the fruits of liberation. (Siṃha Siṃha, folio 415) p.
37) The seed-syllable, joined with the *vyāhṛtis*, is surrounded by two pairs of squares and situated in the corners of the fire-pitcher (*vasu*).
Next, one should write the seed-syllable of Durgā joined with the letters [of the alphabet] and bound by the *gaṇḍa*;
then the Gāyatrī, its openings bound by the power of the Sun; then that [mantra] joined with the Triṣṭubh;
then the seed-syllable with the Mātṛkā; and finally, within a pair of earth-fortresses (*dharāpura*), the true Cintāmaṇi Lion.
This yantra, multiplied by the number of the Sun (twelve) and drawn according to the prescribed method, bestows protection and success;

it generates all forms of good fortune and wards off all enemies. [The meaning of this is: there, as before, having drawn a hexagon, one should draw six triangles within its six junctions so that they become clearly manifest.]

Having drawn another hexagon according to the method taught by the Guru, one should write the seed-syllable of Śakti in its center—accompanied by the object of attainment (sādhya), the practitioner (sādhaka), and the rite—as before; then, one should surround it with the Vyāhṛtis in reverse order. As it has been stated by the Teachers:
One should cause the Śakti to enter by means of the *vyāhṛtis* in reverse order, ending with the semi-vowels (*antasthā*).

Then, having written the seed-syllable of Durgā, *duṃ*, within the interiors of the twelve triangles, one should write the fourth vowel together with the *anusvāra* in those very places. This has been stated by the venerable teacher:
One should now write the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) ending in *ra* (the letter *r*) within the corners of the sun, provided with a *bindu*. Then,
on both sides of each of the twelve triangles, one [syllable] per side, in sequence,
one should write the twenty-four letters of the Vedic *gāyatrī* along with their *bindus*, moving counter-clockwise in a clockwise direction.
One should draw it; and it has been stated by the venerable teachers (Ācāryacaraṇas): "One should write the Gāyatrī in reverse order on the cheeks of the fire.

Then, as before, having written the seed-syllables of Śakti at the tips of the twelve triangles, one should bind them together with each other as before, skipping one at a time. Having fashioned two circles outside of that—
In the path situated between those two:
"Let us press the Soma for Jātavedas; may he burn away the wealth of the one who acts as an enemy.
May Agni carry us across all difficulties, as one crosses a river with a boat, beyond all misfortunes. (Ṛgveda 1.7.7.1)
Thus, one should encircle [the mantra] in reverse order with the syllables of the *triṣṭubh* mantra together with their *bindus*;
as it has been stated by the venerable teachers:
"Furthermore, one should likewise fashion the *triṣṭubh* on the outside."
Regarding this, the explanation of the venerable Śrī Padmapādācārya is as follows: "Likewise, the *triṣṭubh*" means in reverse order.

Then, having encircled [the central syllable] with the *mātṛkā* in direct order and the *mātṛkā* in reverse order as before, one should construct an eight-cornered figure (*aṣṭakoṇa*) outside of that; and as previously described, one should place the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha and the seed-syllable of Cintāmaṇi in their respective corners.
And having drawn it in that same manner, one should fashion it with sixteen spikes; this yantra bestows the aforementioned results.
(Siṃ Siṃ pṛ 416) ||60||
One should draw a lotus with six petals, having inscribed the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) in the center and on the petals as well;
this yantra, surrounded by vowels and placed within an underground chamber, bestows sons upon women.

[The meaning of this is as follows: Having fashioned a six-petalled lotus on birch bark or similar material, having inscribed the seed-syllable of Śakti together with the name of the person to be protected (sādhya) in its center, and having likewise inscribed the seed-syllable of Śakti on all six petals; then, having fashioned two circles outside of that and having encircled the space between them with the sixteen vowels accompanied by the nasal bindu, one should draw a square outside of that.
One should perform this; such is the fruit of the aforementioned yantra. (Siṃ Siṃ pṛ 416) || 61 ||

Having inscribed the Śakti in the center of a hexagon and having again inscribed the name itself in the corners, that yantra—containing the target within it and situated within a city of earth (a square)—becomes a means of subjugating men. (The meaning of this is as before: having fashioned a hexagon, in its center and in its corners [one should inscribe] together with the target...)
Having written the seed-syllable of Śakti, one should draw a square around it; this yantra bestows the aforementioned fruits. (Siṃ Siṃ, p. 416) || 62 ||

The practitioner of mantra should extract the mantra consisting of the three seed-syllables— Vāgbhava (Eṃ), Śambhuvanitā (Hrīṃ), and Ramā-bīja (Śrīṃ)— which is the means for attaining the fruits of the three aims of life. || 63 ||
The knower of mantras should fashion the six limbs of this mantra, joined with their respective seed-syllables, beginning with the Vāgbhava (AIM) and using the six long vowels.
The practitioner should perform the previously mentioned ritual placements (nyāsa) and should also meditate [upon the Goddess] as follows:

her body is crimson like vermilion; she has three eyes; she wears a crown of rubies with the Leader of the Stars (the Moon) shining upon it as her crest-jewel; her face is smiling; and her breasts are full.
One should meditate upon the supreme Mother, who is gentle, holding in her two hands a jeweled goblet filled with gems and a red lotus, and whose left foot rests upon a red jar.

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; the practitioner of mantra should offer oblations ten times that number with milk-rice (pāyasa) soaked in sweet substances, and should worship upon the pedestal previously described.

Having offered oblations to the Goddess with highly beautiful perfumes and other substances according to the previously mentioned method, and with *palāśa* flowers, one shall attain great eloquence and prosperity.
One should drink consecrated *brāhmī* ghee; after one year, one will attain poetic genius (*kavitva*).
By offering oblations of white mustard seeds mixed with salt, the practitioner of mantras shall bring others under his control.
Whether it be a man, a woman, or a king— no deliberation need be made here—
[one should act] with flowers grown from four-finger-widths [of earth], sprinkled with sandalwood water and mixed with ashes. (69)
Having performed the oblation, the practitioner quickly brings even the three worlds under his control;
he should offer ten thousand red lotuses soaked in honey.
A king attains prosperity through rice grains grown from paddy; likewise, he attains the glory of sovereignty through rice grains mixed with sesame seeds.
One should also accomplish the previously mentioned rites by means of this mantra.
This three-syllable vidyā is considered to be Māyā encased by Vāk;
one should arrange it with the middle syllable joined with a long vowel and encased by Vāk.
The knower of mantras should then sequentially assign the limbs (aṅgas) together with their seed-syllables (jātis).
The knower of mantras should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) exactly as it was previously prescribed. 73.

I bow to the eternal goddess Śyāmāṅgī, who bears the moon upon her crest and holds in her own hands the gesture of generosity, a red lotus, a goblet rich with blood, and the supreme boon that dispels all fear.
I bow to the consort of Hara, worshipped by the gods, who rests upon a red lotus, whose breasts are radiant with pearl necklaces, and who is made beautiful by her three eyes. || 74 ||
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with a tenth part of that amount,
using *palāśa* flowers, or flowers from its own blossoms, or flowers from the *rājavṛkṣa* tree, accompanied by sweet substances.
One should worship the Supreme Goddess on the seat established by Hṛllekhā;
the practitioner of mantra should worship Hṛllekhā and the others previously mentioned, beginning from the center.
The practitioner of mantras should worship the couples in the six corners as before;
the worship of the limbs is performed on the filaments, and the Mothers are to be worshipped on the petals.
Mounted upon the lap of Bhairava, with smiling faces and languid with passion,
they are Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, and the one known as Unmatta. (78)
Behind them are the eight Bhairavas, terrifying with skull-bowls, who hold a trident, a skull-cup, a [corpse], and a small drum. 79.

The Mothers are said to begin with long vowels and are adorned with curved locks of hair; the Bhairavas are remembered as beginning with short vowels. They are terrible, clothed in elephant hides, and resplendent. || 80 ||
On the sixteen petals, Karālī and the others previously mentioned are to be worshipped;
outside of that are Anaṅgarūpā and the others, and further outside are the world-protectors (lokeśas) and their weapons.
In this way, one should propitiate the Goddess by following the very path prescribed in the scriptures;
thus, one brings kings under control as well as women languid with passion. 82.
One should offer food with clarified butter and obtains the desired wealth;
having offered fragrant flowers, one attains the desired prosperity.
One should eat food every day that has been consecrated with this mantra;
one will certainly become free from disease and shall attain a long life. (84)

The three-syllable mantra beginning with *pāśa* (the letter *pa*), joined with *ananta* (the letter *a*) and the *bindu*, followed by *māyā* (the letter *ī*), *brahmā* (the letter *ka*), *agni* (the letter *ra*), and *tāra* (the letter *o*), bestows the fruit of bringing all under one's control. [The meaning is clear: *ananta* is the letter *a*; joined with the *bindu*, it becomes *āṃ*. *Māyā* is the goddess Bhuvaneśī, represented by the letter *ī*. *Brahmā* is the letter *ka*. *Agni* is the letter *ra*. *Tāra* is the letter *o*.]*
*Tāra* is the *praṇava*; joined with those two, it becomes *kroṃ*. Here, the name of the first seed-syllable is "noose" (*pāśa*), and the name of the last is "hook" (*aṅkuśa*). || 85 ||
The sages and so forth have been mentioned previously; the ritual application of the limbs is considered to be performed with the seed-syllable (bīja).

I worship that primordial Bhuvaneśvarī, who holds a boon-granting gesture, a goad, a noose, and the gesture of fearlessness in her hands; who is seated upon a lotus throne, possesses three eyes, and resembles ten million rising suns. 87.
Eating only sacrificial food (haviṣya) and having conquered his senses, he should recite the mantra twenty-four hundred thousand times (meaning four million times).
At the conclusion of the recitation, the best of those who know the mantra should perform one thousand oblations.

Then, one should offer oblations with fuel-sticks of milk-tree wood smeared with curd, honey, and ghee— [“madhu” means honey according to Amara], along with pure sesame seeds equal in number to that [total], accompanied by milk.
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship Her upon the seat fashioned from the Hṛllekhā mantra, which is endowed with the nine powers, according to the sequence that will be described.
p.
41) One should first worship Hṛllekhā and the others in the pericarp according to the rule;
the limbs (aṅgas) should be on the filaments, and the Mothers should be placed on the petals in due order. (91)
Furthermore, Indra and the others are to be worshipped, and their weapons outside of them;
by worshipping the Goddess in this manner, one indeed becomes Vaiśravaṇa in person.
He is delighted by all the worlds, resembling the sun in his splendor;
the house presided over by him is filled with the flames of lamps at night.
This is witnessed by all living beings through the power of this mantra.
For the sake of attaining a kingdom, one should perform oblations at night with mustard seeds mixed with parched grain. 94.

The practitioner shall instantly bring a king under his control, as well as the king's wife; by offering oblations of food, he becomes possessed of food, and from the offering of lotuses, he becomes glorious.
By offering flowers produced from the *rājavṛkṣa* tree, one becomes a poet;
by oblation with sesame seeds, one becomes free from disease; and with clarified butter, one shall attain long life. (96)
The best of practitioners should accomplish even those rites previously mentioned,

having drawn the bolts of the eight directions, the three-syllable mantra with the noose and other symbols in the center, the limb-mantras in the compartments, and the mantras in the remaining central spaces.

One should write two mantras of eight syllables. Having written the six letters beginning with *a* and ending with *ca*, followed by the pairs *yu-la* and *ya-ra*, upon the bolts of the seats of space (*vyomāsana*),
one should thereafter write two rows [of letters] in order according to the qualities of Indra, the Lord of Waters, and the others.
Regarding the commentary on the difficult points: "preceded by vowels" (*ac-pūrva*) refers to the vowels (*ac*), excluding the neuter ones.

The first group of six is *a, ā, i, ī, u, ū*; the second group of six is *e, ai, o, au, aṃ, aḥ*. These are joined with the "excellent [syllables] of dissolution" (*layavara*). "Seated upon the throne of space" (*vyomāsana*) means those whose seat or station (*āsana*) is in space (*vyoma*), which is the letter *ha*. [This applies to] Indra, Jalādhipa, and the others.

"East, west," and so forth; "according to the qualities" means by way of the sequence of the three syllables. "Eightfold and sixteen-syllabled" refers to the *māyā* (the letter *ī*) together with the *ātman* (the letter *haṃ*), situated within the pair of vowels. Here, *ātman* is *haṃsa*, and by the word *māyā*, the fourth vowel (*ī*) is to be understood. Thus it is said in the *Nighaṇṭumātṛkā*:
As it is said: "Īstrimūrti, Vāmanetra, Śekhara, Kauṭila, Vāgmī, Śuddha, Jihvākhya, and Māyāviṣṇu are thus revealed.
Regarding the sequence for writing the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) situated within the pair of vowels together with the *ātman* (the letter *a*), it is stated in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:
One should write the five-syllable mantra: the word *haṃsa*, the syllable with the left eye (ī), adorned by a dot and a crescent (*bindu* and *indu*), followed again by the word *haṃsa*.
"Containing within its belly a pair of vowels, it shall consist of seven syllables and be eightfold. Thus [it is said].
Therefore, the seven syllables beginning with *aṃ haṃsaḥ*, *īṃ haṃsaḥ*, and *āṃ* should be written on the filaments (*kesara*) in that order.
This construction of the yantra is also stated in the *Prapañcasāra*:
"The six [syllables] preceded by *a* and ending with *paścāt* (the latter half), joined with *a-vi-ha-la-ya-ra-ya*, situated within the eight directions..."

One should visualize an eight-petaled lotus, its filaments shining with the union of vowels and consonants accompanied by Māyā (the letter *m*), and externally bearing the two groups of eight syllables known as the "Eight-Syllable" and the "Sixteen-Syllable" [mantras] emerging from its corners; in its center, three rows shine forth with the syllables of the noose (*pāśa*), the power (*śakti*), and the goad (*aṅkuśa*).

This supreme yantra, named Ghaṭārgala, consists of the syllables arranged in both direct and reverse order, encircled by the noose (pāśa) and the goad (aṅkuśa), and further surrounded by a lotus and a jar that grants desired fruits and auspiciousness. ||2||

One should write the plow (halam) in the east and west gates, then the horse (hayam) in the southeast and northwest; the syllable *ha* (havārṇa) in the south and north, and the elephant (dvipaṅkti) in the southwest and northeast. || 3 ||
And one should draw a spear (śakti) joined with a noose (pāśa), a goad (aṅkuśa), and the name of the target (sādhya) within the pericarp;
and the six limbs (aṅga) in the inner compartments, and the eight syllables in the remaining ones.
Then, in the sixteen compartments, the practitioner of mantra should likewise place the sixteen-syllable mantra;
and upon the filaments of the lotus, he should likewise place the Māyā [syllable Hrīṃ], which consists of the four vowels and the Ātman [syllable Hūṃ].
On each of the petals, one should enclose the mantras located at the pericarp by means of the seed-syllables of the noose (pāśa) and the goad (aṅkuśa), and likewise on the exterior of the lotus.
One should cause [the syllables] to enter by means of the letters arranged in forward and reverse order on the outside of that;
thereafter, with a jar situated upon a lotus, one should draw a lotus within its opening.
In the *Sārasaṃgraha*:
"The machine known as Ghaṭārgala is supreme for bestowing all prosperity. (97)

In the eight treasuries (kośas), one should write the Māyā-bīja (Hrīṃ) together with its own counterpart, situated within the pair of vowels; on the petals, one should write the root mantra in three rows in succession.
It should be encircled three times by nooses and goads, and surrounded by the letters in both direct and reverse order.
It is surrounded on the outside by a lotus-mouthed jar resting upon a lotus. || 98 ||
This machine, which has a jar as its bolt, is considered a gift for practitioners of mantra;
it consists of the noose (pāśa), the goddess Śrī, Śakti, Kandarpa, Kāma-śakti, and others, as well as the goad (aṅkuśa).
The first mantra consists of eight syllables; thereafter, "Kāmini Rañjini Svāhā" is proclaimed by the wise as another eight-syllable mantra. (100)
*Hrīṃ gauri rudradayite yogeśvari savarma phaṭ*.
This sixteen-syllable mantra, ending with *dviṭha* (svāhā), has been proclaimed by the virtuous. (101)
Having written this mantra according to the prescribed rule within the center of the yantra on birch bark or similar material,
one should wear it on the left arm, around the neck, or upon one's own head.
One shall bring under control all the gods, and mortals especially, as well as kings;
having written this on a blue cloth and made it into a pill, one should then [place it] upon the effigy of the person to be influenced.
One should place her, fashioned from rice-grains, upon the heart;
having cast her into a vessel filled with the three sweets according to the ritual injunctions.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and having cast the bali oblation during the nights,
the practitioner of mantra should daily recite the root mantra eight thousand times.
Within seven days, one shall bring back the desired woman, who will be overwhelmed by passion;
having written this on birch bark and then rolled it into a pill—thus is the specific instruction in the *Śāradātilaka*.
One should wrap [the vessel] in sequence with lac, copper, silver, and gold;
having placed the Goddess Bhuvaneśvarī within that jar, one should worship her according to the prescribed rite.
Having touched it, one should recite the mantra according to the rules one thousand times, O Divākara;
then, having consecrated the beloved person to be accomplished, one should bind the vessel [or yantra] up to the crest.
A person who performs this with speech, body, and mind— having drawn that yantra on a wall— obtains beauty, nourishment, wealth, health, and renown.
One should worship [it] daily with devotion. || 106 ||
Even ghosts, spirits, and demons are not able even to look upon it;
therefore, having drawn this on a helmet, a warrior who wears it shall achieve success.
Having slain many enemies in battle, the king attains victory;

she is to be accomplished within two fire-purified cities marked with thunderbolts, and is accompanied by the noose, goad, and the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons [with the noose and goad held at her belly].
One should repeatedly draw that [design] all around—in the center, in the eight corners, in the city-gate arms, in the lotuses, and again in the outer circle. || 108 ||
Written on birch bark, this shall bestow the fruits of enjoyment and liberation; it brings all men under control, generates health and sovereignty, and grants victory in battles. (Śāradātilaka) 109.
One should draw [the mandala] upon a lotus [or, according to some readings, "upon birch bark" (*bhūrje*)], which is complete, enriched with the gods [i.e.,
the filaments of the vowels (*svarakesarāḍhye*)], possessing eight petals [the eight classes of consonants (*vargāṣṭapatre*)],
and situated at the front of the earth.
One should draw the Māyā, bound by means of the noose and goad according to their qualities and situated in the center together with the sādhya. || 110 ||
This *candradā* yantra is the most excellent of all; when worn, it bestows upon men health, sovereignty, good fortune, victory, and so forth, incessantly. Thus [it is said]. (111)
The Śrībhuvaneśvarī-paṭala, within the Daśavidyā-rahasya of the Śrīrudrayāmala, is complete.
Now begins the ritual manual for the worship of Bhuvaneśvarī.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Now I shall describe the procedure for worship for the sake of attaining all desires and goals.
Having known the Yama, one does not know the imperishable state of the Self. || 1 ||
Thereupon, the illustrious practitioner, having risen from his bed during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, having washed his hands and feet,
and having sat down upon his own seat, [should visualize] within the pericarp of a thousand-petaled white lotus facing downwards on his own head, situated upon a lunar disc, the [deity].

The God of all gods, whose mind is gladdened by the bliss of knowledge, who has three eyes and four arms, holding the gesture of wisdom (*jñānamudrā*), a book, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness; he is embraced with his right arm by his beloved on his left side, who holds a lotus in her left hand and wears red garments and ornaments.
Having meditated upon Him who is the holy site of all holy sites, the most auspicious of all auspicious things, and whose nature is Supreme Śiva;
having visualized oneself bathed by the stream of nectar flowing from His pair of feet;
and having worshipped Him with mental offerings, one should mutter the mantra: *oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ ha sa kha phreṃ ha sa kṣa*.
*Ma la va ra yūṃ hsauṃḥ śauṃḥ*. Having mentally contemplated the *śrīpādukā* of the venerable [Name] Ānandanātha ten times, one should perform a prostration like a staff. As follows:
"I bow to the true Guru, peaceful, manifest, and of the nature of Śiva."
With my head [I bow] to the one seated upon the Yoga-pīṭha for the sake of attaining the goals of liberation and desire. || 1 ||
I bow to the glorious Guru, supreme bliss, whose very form is bliss; by his mere presence, the boon of consciousness-bliss arises.
Salutation to that venerable Guru by whom that state was revealed—the state which is of the form of an unbroken circle and by which the moving and the unmoving are pervaded. || 3 ||
Salutations to that illustrious Guru, by whom the eye was opened for one blinded by the darkness of ignorance, using the medicinal collyrium-stick of knowledge. (4)
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara;
the Guru alone is the entire universe—salutation to that illustrious Guru. || 5 ||
Salutations to you, O Lord, Blessed One, Śiva, in the form of the Guru!
You who have assumed manifold forms through the perfect accomplishment of the descent of knowledge! (6)
Salutations to You, who are ever-new and of ever-new form, whose singular nature is the ultimate reality,
the sun that shatters the darkness of all ignorance, and the mass of pure consciousness.

To the independent one, whose form is fashioned by compassion, the supreme self; to the one who is dependent upon his devotees, appearing in auspicious forms for those who are worthy of liberation. || 8 ||
To the one who is the form of knowledge for the wise, the light for those who illuminate;
to the discernment for the discriminating, and the reflective awareness for those possessed of insight.
In front, on both sides, behind, above, and below, may you always establish your seat through my very mind—indeed, through your inconceivable form. 10.
Thus, having prostrated before the venerable Guru and visualized him as being well-pleased, and having mentally received his command,

one should contemplate the Supreme Śakti upon the Śṛṅgāṭaka-pīṭha situated within the triangle inside the four-petalled lotus of golden hue at the place of the Yoni, in the center of the cavern of the Liṅga at the Mūlādhāra.

Kuṇḍalinī, coiled like a serpent with her face turned upward, possessing three and a half loops, as slender as a lotus fiber, radiant as a thousand rising suns, resembling ten million flashes of lightning,
having the form of the fifty letters and the nature of the thirty-eight kalās, the abode of the three luminous realms.

Having visualized the Goddess of all gods as sleeping within all the mantras, and having rendered her conscious by means of the innate *nāda* taught by the Guru, one awakens her with the staff of sound "Hūṃ. [Although the form "having awakened" (*prabodhya*) alone is pure, it is nevertheless accepted here as it stands, according to the practice of the Tantric scriptures. In that regard:

Having worshipped on the four petals in clockwise order with "Vaṃ Namaḥ," "Śaṃ Namaḥ," "Ṣaṃ Namaḥ," and "Saṃ Namaḥ," and having worshipped in the center with the root mantra (mūla-mantra), one should raise [the deity] everywhere with the mantra "Haṃsa," lead [it] from lotus to lotus, and place it at the base of the liṅga in the six-petaled lotus of the Svādhiṣṭhāna.

Having mounted her upon a coral-colored [lotus] there, one should worship her with "vaṃ namaḥ," "bhaṃ namaḥ," "maṃ namaḥ," "yaṃ namaḥ," "raṃ namaḥ," and "laṃ namaḥ" on the petals, and with the root mantra in the center; then, having raised her everywhere with the mantra "haṃsaḥ," one should lead her to the blue, ten-petaled lotus of the *maṇipūra* at the navel, and there [worship her with] "ḍaṃ."

Having worshipped with "namaḥ ḍhaṃ," "namaḥ ṇaṃ," "namaḥ taṃ," "namaḥ thaṃ," "namaḥ daṃ," "namaḥ dhaṃ," "namaḥ paṃ," and "namaḥ phaṃ" upon the petals, and having worshipped with the root mantra (mūla) in the center, one should then lead her to the twelve-petaled lotus of the *anāhata* cakra in the heart, which is of a tawny color, and there [worship] with "kaṃ namaḥ."
*Khaṃ namaḥ*, *gaṃ namaḥ*, *ghaṃ namaḥ*, *ṅaṃ namaḥ*, *caṃ namaḥ*, *chaṃ namaḥ*, *jaṃ namaḥ*,

*jhaṃ namaḥ*, *ñaṃ namaḥ*, *ṭaṃ namaḥ*, *ṭhaṃ namaḥ*— having thus worshipped [these] on the petals and with the root mantra in the center, one should then [worship] her in the Viśuddhi at the throat, within a sixteen-petaled lotus of smoky color.

Having led [the deity] there, one should worship with "aṃ namaḥ," "āṃ namaḥ," "iṃ namaḥ," "īṃ namaḥ," "uṃ namaḥ," "ūṃ namaḥ," "ṛ namaḥ," "ṝ namaḥ," "ḷṃ namaḥ," "ḹṃ namaḥ," "eṃ namaḥ," "aiṃ namaḥ," "oṃ namaḥ," "auṃ namaḥ," "aḥ namaḥ," and "aṃ namaḥ" upon the petals, and in the center with the root mantra (mūla), and then—

Having led her to the *ājñācakra* at the center of the eyebrows— a two-petaled lotus with the color of lightning— one should worship her there between the petals with "Haṃ Namaḥ" and "Kṣaṃ Namaḥ," and also with the root mantra. Then,
[one proceeds] to the supreme *bindu* situated within the triangle in the center of the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus located in the *brahmarandhra*.
Having satiated her with the supreme nectar (*paramāmṛta*), one should then become intent on hearing the *nāda* (sound) and contemplate absorption (*laya*) for one *muhūrta*.
At the time of descending, reciting the mantra "I am that" (*so'haṃ*) everywhere, one should descend from lotus to lotus;
mentally, following the sequence of the *ājñācakra* and the rest, one should worship within each respective lotus with their corresponding syllables.

Having satiated each respective support, each respective channel, and each respective presiding deity with that nectar, and having likewise established them in their own place at the *mūlādhāra*, one should prostrate, [reciting]:
"She who was manifest during the first departure, and who has become nectar once again during the return..."
I take refuge in that woman whose form is bliss, who wanders along the inner path.
Having thus meditated upon the form of the Goddess, one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) according to the procedure to be described;

then, having again performed the *ṛṣi*-assignment and the other [assignments], as well as the six-limbed assignment (*kara-ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*), and having offered the recitation (*japa*), one should offer one's own action.
"I am the Goddess, and I am none other; I am Brahman alone, not subject to sorrow.
I am of the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss"—thus one should contemplate one's own Self.
Whatever I do from morning until evening, and from evening until morning, O Source of the Universe, may that be an act of worship unto you.
Having thus offered [myself], for the performance of my own duties:

"O Supreme Mistress, O Bhuvaneśvarī, who consists of the consciousness of the three worlds, having risen at dawn by the very command of your feet, I shall conduct the journey of worldly existence for your pleasure. (1)
O Śrī Bhuvaneśvarī, O Sovereign Lady, as I continue upon the journey of saṃsāra according to Your command, may rivalry, contempt, negligence, and fear not overcome me, O Mother. (2)
I know what is right, yet I have no inclination toward it; I know what is wrong, yet I have no aversion to it.
O Hṛṣīkeśa, I act exactly as I am directed by you who abide within my heart.

Having thus requested the command of the Goddess, one should offer the resolve for the *ajapājapa*— which is spontaneously accomplished— to the respective deities: "Today [or] yesterday, throughout the day and night, I have performed the *ajapājapa*, consisting of inhalations and exhalations,
numbering twenty-one thousand six hundred."

In the *mūlādhāra*, *svādhiṣṭhāna*, *maṇipūraka*, *anāhata*, *viśuddha*, *ājñā*, and *brahmarandhra* [cakras], which possess four petals, six petals, ten petals, twelve petals, sixteen petals, two petals, and a thousand petals respectively;

Salutations; I offer [this] according to their respective portions to the sandals of Gaṇapati, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, the individual self (jīvātman), the supreme self (paramātman), and the venerable Guru, who abide within those [lotuses] possessing the colors of gold, coral, blue, tawny, smoke-colored, lightning, and camphor.
Six hundred [recitations] for Gaṇanātha, six thousand for Pitāmaha, six thousand for Gadāpāṇi, and six thousand for Pinākin. || 1 ||
One should give one thousand to oneself, one thousand to the Supreme Self (Paramātman), and one thousand to the Guru; this is the offering according to the prescribed number.

Having thus made this resolve, one should offer it as follows: *Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, I offer six hundred repetitions of the Ajapā-mantra unto Mahāgaṇapati residing in the Mūlādhāra-cakra; salutations.* *Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, [I offer] the repetitions of the Ajapā-mantra unto Brahmā residing in the Svādhiṣṭhāna-cakra...*

I offer six thousand [repetitions], obeisance! Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, I offer six thousand repetitions of the *ajapā* to Viṣṇu, who resides in the *maṇipūra-cakra*, obeisance! Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, I offer six thousand repetitions of the *ajapā* to Rudra, who resides in the *anāhata-cakra*, obeisance! Oṃ...

Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I offer one thousand recitations of the *ajapā* to the individual soul (*jīvātman*) residing in the *viśuddhi-cakra*; obeisance! Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I offer one thousand recitations of the *ajapā* to the supreme soul (*paramātman*) residing in the *ājñā-cakra*; obeisance! Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ.

"I offer one thousand repetitions of the *ajapā* to the venerable sandals of the Guru residing in the center of the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus; obeisance. Having thus offered the *ajapā* recitation and performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the *ajapā* mantra, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "Oṃ, of this venerable [mantra]..."

The deity is the illustrious Paramahaṃsa; *haṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *saḥ* is the power (*śakti*), *so'haṃ* is the pin (*kīlaka*), the principle of *Oṃ* is the station (*sthāna*), the color is golden, the accent is acute (*udātta*), and the application (*viniyoga*) is for my sake in the recitation for the purpose of liberation.
Having thus remembered with palms joined in reverence, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*): *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ* to the Seer (*ṛṣi*) who is the Self of the *Haṃsa*.

Salutation to the Unmanifest Gāyatrī metre on the head; salutation to the deity Śrī Paramahaṃsa on the face; salutation to the seed-syllable *haṃ* on the heart; salutation to the power (*śakti*) *saḥ* on the private parts; salutation to the *kīlaka* "so'haṃ" on the feet;
salutation to the principle of the syllable *oṃ* on the navel; salutation to the acute accent (*udātta-svara*) on the heart; salutation to the ether (*nabhas*) on the throat.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with "Salutation to Sthāna on the head; *hamaḥ* to the golden-colored one on all limbs," one should also perform the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) placement of the hands: *Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hsāṃ*, salutation to the thumbs, the essence of the Sun; *Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hsīṃ*, salutation to the index fingers, the essence of the Moon.
Svāhā! Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hsūṃ, salutation to the Self that is stainless (nirañjanātmane) with the two middle fingers; Vaṣaṭ!

Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hsaiṃ, salutation to the Self that is without appearance (nirābhāsātmane) with the two ring fingers; Huṃ! Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hsauṃ, salutation to the Self that impels the subtle body (tanusūkṣmāpracodayātmane) with the two little fingers; Vauṣaṭ! Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ...
Śrīṃ Hsaṃḥ, to the Self of Unmanifest Consciousness, Phaṭ with the palms and backs of the hands. (p.
48) Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hsāṃ, to the Self of the Sun, obeisance to the heart. Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hsīṃ.
Oṃ ātmane śirase svāhā. Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hsūṃ nirañjanātmane śikhāyai vaṣaṭ.
Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hsaiṃ nirābhāsātmane kavacāya huṃ. Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hsauṃ tanusūkṣmāpracodayātmane netratrayāya vauṣaṭ. Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hsaṃḥ.
Having performed the *kara-ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa* with the mantra "To the weapon, the self of the unmanifest, phaṭ," one should perform the meditation:
"The Brahmins declare Him whose head is heaven, whose navel is the sky, and whose two eyes are the moon and the sun."
He whose ears are the quarters of space and whose feet are the earth—he, the inner self of all beings, is to be meditated upon.

Having thus meditated upon the nature of Virāṭ and contemplated and recited the syllable *h-s-aṃḥ*— which consists of the exit and entry of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*)— twenty-five times, and having offered it according to the path instructed by the Guru,
one should [remain] as some manifestation of consciousness (*cidvilāsa*) with all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) cast off, preceded by the contemplation of the inner sound (*nāda*).

Reflecting, "I am proceeding," for the sake of performing his own duty: "O Goddess whose girdle is the ocean, whose breasts are the mountains, O Consort of Viṣṇu, salutations to you; forgive my touch of your feet."

Having thus prayed to the earth and placed his foot upon it following the movement of his breath, he went outside, discharged urine and feces, performed purification according to the prescribed method, and brushed his teeth.
Then, having gone to a river or similar place, [he recited]: *klīṃ kāmadevāya sarvajanapriyāya namaḥ* (Oblation to Kāmadeva, who is dear to all people), and performed the Vedic [rites].

Having completed the ritual bath, one should begin the Tantric practice. Therein, first, having sipped water (ācamana) with the mantras: "Oṃ, the Root-mantra to the Ātma-tattva, Svāhā; the Root-mantra to the Vidya-tattva, Svāhā; the Root-mantra to the Śiva-tattva, Svāhā," [one should continue] with "Oṃ, today... and so forth, in such-and-such month...

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "On such a fortnight, on such a lunar day, on such a day of the week, under such a constellation, conjunction, and moment, I, [Name] Śarmā, for the pleasure of the Supreme Deity, shall perform the ritual of Tantric bathing," one should draw a triangular wheel in the water from the solar orb (*sūryamaṇḍala*).
Oṃ! O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī—be present in these waters!
Having thus invoked the *tīrtha* with this "impure" (*akuśa*) mudrā and joined it with the *tīrtha* prepared in front, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*),

sprinkle oneself with the root mantra (*mūla*), and while reciting the root mantra, invoke the Goddess from the center of the heart-lotus into the midst of the *tīrtha*. Having meditated upon her there, one should bathe the Goddess three times with the water-pot (*kumbha*) mudrā.
Having established [the deity] in one's own heart and having blocked the seven apertures, one should submerge and emerge three times. Thus is the bath.

49) Now, the twilight ritual (*saṃdhyā*). Having performed the sipping of water (*ācamana*) on the riverbank as before, having performed the root-prāṇāyāma of one’s own [deity], and having invoked the sacred ford (*tīrtha*), one places water in the left hand, covers it with the right hand, and [recites] *laṃ vaṃ raṃ yaṃ*.

Having consecrated [the water] three times with the syllable "Haṃ," reciting the root mantra while forming the *tattvamudrā*, he should sprinkle it seven times upon his head with the root mantra. Then, placing the remaining water in his right hand and meditating on it as being of the nature of light,
he should draw it in through the *iḍā* [nāḍī], wash away the sins within his body, and [visualize] that water as black-colored and in the form of sin.
Having reflected thus, Piṅgalā, having purified [the area] in front, should cast [the offering] onto the previously prepared diamond-stone (*vajraśilā*) with the mantra "phaṭ.

Then, lifting up the *arghya* vessel, one should say: "Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ haṃ saḥ, to the venerable Kula-Mārtaṇḍa-Bhairava, together with the Power of Radiance (*prakāśaśakti*), I offer this *arghya*; obeisance!"

Having thus offered the *arghya* three times to the Kula-sūrya, one should lead the Goddess into the solar disc within the lotus of one's own heart, meditate upon her there according to the prescribed rule, and recite the root *gāyatrī*: "We know Dhanadā; we meditate on Ratipriyā;
hrīṃ, may that Svāhā inspire us. Having recited this *gāyatrī* three times while also chanting the root mantra, [one should proceed].

Having offered the *arghya* to the Root Goddess with the mantra: "To the venerable Bhuvaneśvarī, together with her limbs (*sāṅgāyai*), together with her retinue (*saparivārāyai*), together with her vehicle (*savāhanāyai*), and accompanied by her power (*śaktisahitāyai*), I offer this *arghya*; obeisance, svāhā," and having recited the root mantra as many times as possible, one should then perform *prāṇāyāma*.
One should bring [the breath] back to its own place. Thus ends the twilight ritual (saṃdhyā).

Now, the libation (*tarpaṇa*). Having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) as before, and having executed the *prāṇāyāma*, the assignment of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, and the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), one again invokes the sacred site (*tīrtha*). Having consecrated the water seven times with the root mantra using the nectar-gesture (*amṛtamudrā*), one establishes and draws the root diagram (*mūlayantra*) within that water, and [invokes] the Goddess there from her own heart.

Having brought [the Guru] along with his retinue, having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa through the application of the six-limbed mantra (ṣaḍaṅgamantra), and having consecrated him with nectar through the practice of Kuṇḍalinī, one should worship him according to rule with perfumes and other offerings, and satisfy the Guru in the northeast with this: "Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, may the venerable Śrī Amukānandanātha be satisfied."
Having satisfied [the deities] three times, one should satisfy [the gurus] as follows: to the southeast, three times with "Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ may the supreme guru (paramaguru) be satisfied";

to the north, three times with "Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ may the preceptor-guru (parameṣṭhiguru) be satisfied"; and all around, three times with "Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ may the gurus of the divine lineage (divyaugha) be satisfied," and three times with "Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ may the gurus of the perfected lineage (siddhaugha) be satisfied."

Having offered libations three times with "Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, may the gurus of the Mānavaugha be satisfied," and having again offered libations three times to the Root Goddess according to the previously mentioned method, one should offer libations in sequence to the retinue as prescribed for the Yantra;
then, having performed the breath control (prāṇāyāma), the assignment of seers (ṛṣyādi), and the six-limbed ritual placement (kara-ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa), [one should worship] the Root Goddess.

Having released [the deity] and established it within one's own heart, and having placed the sacred water (tīrtha) in its own place, one should dismiss it into the solar orb. Thus ends the libation (tarpaṇa).
Now, the entry into the house: Having arrived at the sacrificial hall, one should sprinkle the deities of the doorway with water and other substances,
and worship them with scents, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and so forth— *oṃ dhaṃ dhātre namaḥ* on the right, *oṃ viṃ vidhātre namaḥ* on the left,
*oṃ gaṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ* on the right, *oṃ yaṃ yamunāyai namaḥ* on the left, and [to the deity] above.
Oṃ glauṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati. Oṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to Dvāraśrī (the Goddess of the Door).
Below: Oṃ daṃ, obeisance to Dehalī (the Threshold). Above: Oṃ vaṃ, obeisance to Vāstupuruṣa (the Architectural Deity). Below: [Oṃ vaṃ, obeisance to Vāstupuruṣa].
Having worshipped the door with "Obeisance to Ananta," having scattered unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) inside the sacrificial hall, and having joined his palms in reverence (*añjali*), [he recites]:
"Whatever rite has been begun by me, whatever I shall do, and whatever has already been done..."
O Goddess, out of compassion, always make all of that free from obstacles for me.

Having thus paid homage, preceded by the inhalation and exhalation of the breath and accompanied by the contraction of the left side of the body, one should cause [the deity] to enter the center of the house with the mantra: "Obeisance to Vāstvadhipati; obeisance to Dīpanātha in the northeast. O Dīpanātha, O Guru, O Lord, O Leader of the Teacher’s Self!"
And you ought to grant permission for the worship of Bhuvaneśvarī.
Having lit a ghee lamp in the northeast, one should offer obeisance to Bhairava in the southwest with the mantra: "Obeisance to Bhairava!
O extremely fierce one, [alternatively 'sharp-fanged one'] of great body, you who resemble the fire at the end of an aeon!"
Salutations to you, O Bhairava; you should deign to grant me permission.

Having lit an oil lamp in the southwest and made this prayer, one should visualize the place of worship as twofold and say, "Obeisance to the place for my own seat. Then, having visualized the place for the Goddess's seat as twofold, one should worship that place, saying, "Obeisance to the place for the Goddess's seat. Now, the manner of the seats: *Oṃ, obeisance to the Tortoise Seat; Huṃ*.
Salutation to the Foundation Power (Ādhāra-śakti). Oṃ, salutation to the seat of Brahmā; Oṃ, salutation to the lotus seat;
Oṃ, salutation to the stainless seat; Oṃ, salutation to the seat of Ananta; Oṃ, salutation to the Brahma-lotus seat;
Oṃ, salutation to the seat of Garuḍa; Oṃ, salutation to the yoga seat; Oṃ, salutation to the supreme lion-throne of Śrī Parātpara.

Having worshipped with the word "Namaḥ" using perfumes and unbroken rice grains (akṣata), one should make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "Oṃ, for the mantra 'Pṛthivī...', Merupṛṣṭha is the seer (ṛṣi), Kūrma is the deity, Sutala is the meter (chanda), and its application (viniyoga) is upon the seat. Having thus resolved and placed the hand upon the ground, one should recite the mantra:
"Oṃ! O Earth, by you the worlds are supported; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu.
You, O Goddess, support me; make this seat pure.
Having thus spread a seat of wool or other materials with the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to Bhūmi," [one should place] upon it [the lotus] within the six corners.

Having written the seed-syllable *bhūḥ* in the center and inscribed the syllable *huṃ*, one should sit there; then, having supplicated the Guru at the *brahmarandhra* with the *saṃghaṭṭamudrā*, one should prostrate, saying: "Guṃ, obeisance to the Gurus; Paṃ, obeisance to the Supreme Gurus;
Paṃ, obeisance to the Gurus higher than the supreme; Paṃ, obeisance to the Parameṣṭhi Gurus."

Having prostrated, saying: "Gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati on the right; Duṃ, obeisance to Durgā on the left; obeisance to Bhairava at the back; obeisance to Baṭuka-Hanumān in front; Śrī Bhuvaneśvarī, obeisance in the heart. (p. 51)
Now, the binding of the directions beginning with the east: "Homage to Indra in the east; homage to Agni in the southeast; homage to Yama in the south;
homage to the Rākṣasa in the southwest; homage to Varuṇa in the west; homage to Pavana in the northwest; homage to Kubera in the north; homage to Īśvara in the northeast; [homage] above."

Salutation to Brahmā; salutation to Ananta in the netherworld (pātāla). Having performed the three *tāla* gestures, one should contemplate oneself in the form of the deity and perform all the preparatory rites (*sādhana*).

Now follows the ritual application (*prayoga*): for the sake of pleasing the venerable Bhuvaneśvarī, [the performance of] recitation (*japa*), worship (*arcana*), and fire-oblation (*homa*) of this [mantra].

"I shall do it. Having bowed to his own guru, the mantra-practitioner, with face turned upward, strikes the sides and claps his hands, terrifying all spirits: "May those beings depart who dwell upon the earth!"
May those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva.
May those spirits and piśācas depart in every direction; without causing them any offense, I shall commence this rite of Brahman.
Having thus performed the dissolution of the elements by means of the manifestation of one's own consciousness-nature, the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) proceeds as follows:
from the feet up to the knees is the earth mandala, square and yellow in color;
from the knees up to the navel is the water mandala, shaped like a half-moon and white in color.
Having meditated upon the fire-mandala, triangular and red in color, from the navel to the heart;
then having meditated upon the wind-mandala, hexagonal and smoke-colored, from the heart to the space between the eyebrows;
and [finally] the space-mandala, circular and black in color, from the space between the eyebrows to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra).
Having meditated [on the deity], one should visualize the Person of Sin (pāpapuruṣa) in the left side of the belly:
"Brahmin-slaughter is his head and shoulders; theft of gold his two arms;
drinking liquor is joined with his heart; and violating the Guru’s bed his two hips."
That pair of feet joined together was a destroyer of limbs and minor members;
its hairs were secondary sins, and its beard and eyes were red.
One should visualize the Evil One, bearing a sword and shield, the size of a thumb,
